Discharge Summary:

Patient Information:

Name: [redacted]
Gender: Female	 
DOB: [redacted]	 
Hospital ID: [redacted]

Hospital Course: 

The patient was admitted due to chronic anicteric cholestasis and worsening cough with exertional dyspnea. She was diagnosed with chronic Budd-Chiari syndrome (BCS) complicating sarcoidosis, which was confirmed by histopathological examination of the liver, gastric, and skin biopsies. The patient received treatment with oral prednisolone and warfarin anticoagulation therapy, and was discharged in stable condition.

Summary of Findings:

- Diabetes mellitus evolving for 3 years, without a history of oral contraceptive therapy.
- Increased cholestatic enzymes, including a γ-glutamyl transferase level of 136 UI/L and alkaline phosphatase (ALP) of 325 UI/L.
- Normocytic inflammatory anemia with hemoglobin of 10.6 g/dL, mean corpuscular volume of 82.8 fL, and serum ferritin of 150 g/L.
- Hepatomegaly with hypertrophied caudate lobe, splenomegaly, and porto-systemic collateral circulation, as confirmed by abdominal ultrasound with Doppler and abdominal CT.
- Multinodular liver, absence of hepatic veins, centrolobular hepatocytes that were focally atrophic and replaced by fibrous and inflammatory septa, and fibrosis, as confirmed by abdominal CT and liver biopsy.
- Mediastinal and hilar adenopathies with multiple micronodular opacities on the lower pulmonary lobes, as confirmed by chest CT.
- Non-caseating granuloma on gastric biopsies and sarcoid granulomas on skin lesion biopsies, without damage to bile ducts, as confirmed by histopathological examination.
- Raised angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE) of 201 UECA.
- Negative results for tuberculin testing and bronchoalveolar lavage.

Hospital Course:

The patient was started on oral prednisolone at a dose of 1 mg/kg and warfarin anticoagulation therapy. Additional examinations were performed to screen for an underlying thrombophilic disorder but failed to ascertain an underlying prothrombotic condition. The diagnosis of BCS complicating sarcoidosis was the most likely. The patient responded well to the treatment and was discharged in stable condition.

Discharge:

The patient was discharged in stable condition with instructions for continuing oral prednisolone and warfarin anticoagulation therapy. Follow-up appointments were scheduled with the primary care physician and specialist providers. The patient was advised to monitor symptoms and report any changes or concerns. The patient and their family were counseled on the importance of adherence to medications, lifestyle modifications, and attendance at scheduled appointments.

Discharge Summary

Patient: [Name], Female, 26 years old

Admission Date: [Date]
Discharge Date: [Date]

Chief Complaint: Profound hearing loss in the left ear, tinnitus, and dizziness

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted to our department in 2011 with a complaint of profound hearing loss in her left ear. She also reported experiencing tinnitus and dizziness. She did not have nystagmus during physical examination, and advanced vestibular tests were not conducted. Tonal audiometry revealed a 37-dB hearing loss in the left ear with 70% speech discrimination, while the right ear showed normal range pure tone audiometry.

Radiological examinations showed a left cerebellopontine angle (CPA) mass that encased the left VIII cranial nerve. A key finding was a 4 mm diameter lesion in the internal auditory canal (IAC), also with radiological features corresponding to a left CPA lipoma. The patient was followed up clinically and radiologically for two years, during which time there was no progression of the lipoma.

Diagnosis: Left cerebellopontine angle (CPA) lipoma

The patient was discharged in a stable condition.

Discharge Instructions and Follow-up:

The patient is advised to undergo routine follow-up with an otolaryngologist, as per their physician's instructions.

Follow-up Imaging: CT/MRI after the physician prescribes.

Signed,

[Physician], MD

records.source_note:
Discharge Summary:

Patient Identification:
The patient is a 57-year-old male with a history of extensive tobacco use, nonischemic cardiomyopathy, and an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status (PS) of 3.

Hospital Course:
The patient received mechanical cardiac support with an LVAD due to severe heart failure after successfully completing initial evaluation. Three months after the surgery, mediastinal widening was noted on a chest X-ray performed for dyspnea and cough. CT scans revealed mediastinal lymphadenopathy without evidence of disease outside the chest. Mediastinoscopy was performed and pathologic examination showed consistent SCLC. 

Treatment Strategy:
The patient was removed from active consideration for cardiac transplantation. Chemotherapy was administered while hospitalized for close monitoring. Carboplatin and IV etoposide were given. After his first cycle of chemotherapy, the patient elected not to receive further chemotherapy and workup.

Complications:
The treatment course was complicated by cellulitis, neutropenic fevers with pseudomonas aeruginosa infection, and protracted nausea and vomiting. The patient was treated with a prolonged IV antibiotic course. Although the renal function remained within normal limits, the patient developed signs of worsening overload with left-sided pleural effusion and peripheral edema. 

Outcome: 
The patient elected for hospice care and was discharged home. The patient passed away about 6 months after the administration of chemotherapy.

1. Patient is a 72-year-old female with right breast carcinoma and enlarged axillary lymph nodes.
2. She received neoadjuvant therapy with aromatase inhibitor and CDK4/6 inhibitor.
3. Adjuvant radiation therapy was delivered to the right breast and supraclavicular region.
4. During RTX, she experienced moderate acute radiodermatitis and submammary moist epitheliolysis.
5. Post-radiation, she developed a 2cm circumscribed cutis edema covering former irradiation fields.
6. Biopsy confirmed postradiogenic circumscribed scleroderma (morphea) with fibrosis and chronic inflammation.
7. Despite treatment attempts, the condition persisted for over two years.
8. Patient declined systemic therapies and sought symptomatic management.
9. Discharge instructions include sun protection and sunscreen application.
10. Follow-up appointments are scheduled to monitor disease progression.
records.source_note:
[Discharge Summary]

Admission Date: [Date]
Discharge Date: [Date]

Patient Name: [Patient Name]  Age: 72  Sex: Female

Patient was admitted to the hospital for carcinoma of the right breast with enlarged axillary lymph nodes. She was given neoadjuvant systemic therapy with the nonsteroidal aromatase inhibitor anastrozole (Arimidex®) and the CDK 4/6 inhibitor abemaciclib (Verzenio®) as part of a clinical trial (NeoMONARCH). Following this, adjuvant radiotherapy (RTX) of the right breast and the supraclavicular region was done in three-dimensional (3D) conformal technique. During the course of radiation, the patient developed a moderate acute radiodermatitis with small circumscribed moist epitheliolysis in the submammary fold.

After completion of RTX, the patient developed a 2cm wide circumscribed cutis edema at the irradiated breast, which later grew to cover the whole former irradiation field, with a continuous inflammatory infiltrate, hyperpigmentation, induration, and a loss of breast volume. To rule out a recurrence of lymphangiosis carcinomatosa cutis, a targeted punch biopsy was performed. The histology showed no signs of malignant tumor cells but a pronounced dermal fibrosis with thickened dermis and fibrosis extending into the underlying fatty tissue, with corresponding panniculitis and pronounced chronic perivascular inflammation.

After re-examination, the patient was diagnosed with postradiogenic circumscribed scleroderma 20 months after RTX. The patient declined suggested treatments, which included systemic immune suppression with steroids and methotrexate (MTX) but sought relief through the use of topical steroids and lymph drainage at a specialized center. The clinical picture has remained unchanged since December 2017. 

Instructions were given for the patient to be followed closely with scheduled checkups and monitoring. The patient was discharged with follow-up care plan. Informed consent was provided for the follow-up treatment plan. 

Discharge Diagnosis:
- Postradiogenic circumscribed scleroderma (morphea)

Discharge Condition:
- Stable

Discharge Medications:
- [None provided]

Discharge Instructions:
- The patient should check in with her doctors for scheduled checkups
- The patient should regularly monitor the condition of the affected areas 
- The patient should avoid sun exposure and always apply sunscreen on the affected areas.

The healthcare professional provided instructions for the patient to be followed closely with scheduled checkups and monitoring, and to avoid sun exposure while always applying sunscreen on the affected areas. However, no information was given regarding the patient's treatment plan or medications upon discharge.

Hospital Course:
The patient is a 57-year-old female with medical history significant for epilepsy during childhood, haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes and low platelets syndrome during both pregnancies, proteinuria at the age of 40, sensorineural hearing loss, diabetes mellitus, renal failure, and hypertension at the age of 41. A kidney biopsy revealed IgA nephropathy, while a mutation was found 4 years post-kidney transplantation. The patient is currently stable with mild microalbuminuria and is using prednisone and tacrolimus as immunosuppressants.

Discharge Diagnosis:
IgA nephropathy, diabetes mellitus, hypertension, end-stage renal disease

Hospital Course Summary:
The patient was admitted due to post-kidney transplantation follow-up evaluation. Upon admission, the patient complained of central scotoma causing visual problems. A thorough medical history revealed significant medical problems in the past, including epilepsy, haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes and low platelets syndrome during both pregnancies, sensorineural hearing loss, proteinuria, diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and renal failure. A kidney biopsy performed three years after the first diagnosis revealed IgA nephropathy, which led to the need for peritoneal dialysis. The patient received a kidney transplant from a postmortem, heart-beating donor at the age of 52. Two years after the kidney transplant, the patient presented with severe left ventricle hypertrophy and diastolic heart failure, which remained stable four years after transplantation. Four years post-transplantation, the m.3243A>G mutation was found, with a heteroplasmy level in leucocytes of 6%. 

Upon discharge, the patient was found to have stable kidney function with mild microalbuminuria. The patient was prescribed prednisone and tacrolimus as immunosuppressants and recommended follow-up with her nephrologist.

Admission Date: [Date]
Discharge Date: [Date]

Reason for Admission:
The patient was admitted to the hospital due to multiple cervicofacial lacerations caused by a broken beer bottle. He presented with a blood pressure of 70/40 mmHg, pulse of 110 beats/minute, and hemoglobin level of 4.7 mg/dl.

Hospital Course:
Upon admission, the patient was diagnosed with a suspected vascular injury in neck zone II. CT angiography was performed and showed contrast leakage in the right internal carotid artery. Angiography via the right femoral artery was performed and showed extravasation of contrast media in neck zone III. A stent was inserted at the laceration site, and the patient underwent surgery to remove the hematoma and check for any other injuries. The day after stent insertion, angiography showed no contrast leakage in the right internal carotid artery.

Clinical Findings:
The patient's laceration site was explored, and the hematoma was removed. Furthermore, no other injuries were found. After 12 months of follow-up observation at our outpatient clinic, the patient received antiplatelet medication. No special findings were observed during observation.

Condition and Disposition:
The patient's condition has improved significantly, and he has been discharged from the hospital. He has also been advised to continue antiplatelet medication and to attend follow-up appointments at our outpatient clinic.

The patient's condition has improved and has since been discharged, with follow-up observation and antiplatelet medication advised.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY:

Patient Name: [redacted]
Date of Admission: [redacted]
Date of Discharge: [redacted]

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 29-year-old white male farmer, was admitted to our hospital with the chief complaint of left upper-quadrant abdominal discomfort and unintentional weight loss. On initial examination, he was found to have splenomegaly and laboratory analysis revealed a high leukocyte count, low hemoglobin level, and high platelet count. Further tests revealed the presence of CML in chronic phase and he was initiated on hydroxyurea, which was later substituted with imatinib.

The patient showed a slow progression of splenomegaly until spleen regression was achieved within 3 months of imatinib therapy. The initial reevaluation at 3 months showed no symptoms and weight gain. However, imatinib was discontinued after 6 months due to pancytopenia. Bone marrow study revealed complete remission of CML and numerous Leishmania amastigotes within the macrophages. Treatment with pentavalent antimonials was initiated which led to complete recovery of symptoms and examinations after 60 days of therapy.

While the patient resumed TKI therapy, acute cardiac toxicity required suspension from treatment. Medication was stopped when his heart rate dropped below 45 beats per minute and was replaced by amphotericin B regimen. After 3 months, TKI therapy was resumed and the last PCR showed deep molecular response.

CML in chronic phase, pancytopenia, leishmaniasis, acute cardiac toxicity

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]  

Date of Admission: [REDACTED] 
Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]

Patient Information:

The patient is a 46-year-old male who was admitted with B-symptoms, recurrent pneumonia and lymphadenopathy. A computed tomography (CT) scan showed enlarged liver and spleen, and several lymph nodes including mediastinal and inguinal lymph nodes. He was diagnosed with CD hyaline vascular type and treated with six cycles of R-CHOP chemotherapy. 

Hospital Course:

After the fourth cycle of chemotherapy, a regular follow-up CT scan was conducted which showed dilation of the posterior portion of both main pulmonary arteries more prominent on the right with wall thickening, and an enlargement of hilar and subcarinal lymph nodes. The patient developed hemoptysis and lesions on his legs after the fifth cycle, which were later diagnosed as erythema nodosum. The patient was diagnosed with Behcet’s Disease and was started on hydrocortisone, azathioprine, and enoxaparin.

Discharge Diagnosis:

Behcet’s Disease with a pulmonary aneurysm.

Discharge Medications:

The patient is currently taking prednisone, azathioprine, colchicine, and rivaroxaban.

Follow-up:

The patient is following up with rheumatology outpatient department and doing well with no recurrence of ulcers or signs of active disease as per last appointment.

This discharge summary provides detail about the patient's hospital course and summary of the diagnosis and treatments. The patient received treatment for Behcet’s Disease and is doing well. A follow-up appointment with the rheumatology outpatient department is scheduled.

records.source_note:
Hospital Course: 
The patient presented with complaints of burning, itching, pain, stinging, lacrimation, and decreased vision in her left eye. She reported sand splash to her eyes at the seaside three months prior and had discontinued contact lens wear ten days before admission to the clinic. Biomicroscopic examination of the left eye revealed central keratitis and corneal scraping sample was taken and inoculated for testing. Acanthamoeba sp. cysts were identified in the direct Giemsa stained specimen of corneal scraping. 

Treatment: 
The patient was treated with alternating topical fortified vancomycin, ceftazidime, propamidine isothionate 0.1% and chlorhexidine at ophthalmology clinic. Contact lenses and contact lens solution could not be cultured since they had been disposed of by the patient.

Follow-up: 
At the 2nd month visit, no growth was identified after inoculation of corneal scraping specimen onto E. coli plated NNA agar. The corneal scraping specimen was defined as "T2" genotype "A. castellani" according to PCR and sequence analysis that targeted 18S rDNA region performed. 

Conclusion: 
The patient's case report was approved by the Ethics Committee at Uludag University Faculty of Medicine (2016-9/18), and informed consent was obtained from the patient.

The treatment plan included alternating topical fortified vancomycin, ceftazidime, propamidine isothionate 0.1% and chlorhexidine.

records.source_note:
Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [redacted]
Medical Record Number: [redacted]
Admission Date: [redacted]
Discharge Date: [redacted]
Admitting Diagnosis: Pituitary germinoma
Discharge Diagnosis: Pituitary germinoma, central diabetes insipidus
Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted to the hospital due to an eight-month history of generalized fatigue, increased thirst, increased urinary frequency and volume, reduced nocturnal erections, decreased sexual desire, weight loss of 18 kg in six months, dry skin, cold intolerance, and constipation. The patient was referred to the endocrinology clinic where physical examination revealed normal vital signs and delayed tendon reflex of the deep tendon reflex in the upper/lower extremities. The initial laboratory examination revealed hypopituitarism, hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, polyuria, and hypertonic hypernatremia. The initial MRI scan showed a right-sided pituitary microadenoma. The patient was started on hydrocortisone and levothyroxine replacement therapy. Follow-up studies revealed an abnormal thickening of the infundibulum on the second MRI scan with no evidence of the microadenoma. New laboratory examination results confirmed the previous findings and ruled out the presence of autoimmune or inflammatory conditions. Tumor markers for germ cell tumors were negative. A water deprivation test confirmed central diabetes insipidus. Testosterone replacement and desmopressin (DDAVP) were added to the patient's therapy regimen. A tissue biopsy taken during transsphenoidal surgery revealed a positive result for an intrasellar pituitary germinoma confirmed by positive human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) staining, C-kit, and placental alkaline phosphatase (PLAP). A lumbar MRI scan and lumbar puncture were negative for metastatic disease. The patient was treated with whole ventricle brain radiation and showed subsequent clinical improvement. The patient was stable at the time of discharge.

Discharge Medications:
Hydrocortisone, levothyroxine, testosterone replacement, desmopressin (DDAVP)

Follow-up:
The patient is scheduled for follow-up visits with the endocrinology clinic to monitor treatment and evaluate persistent symptoms. Further imaging studies and laboratory tests may be ordered as indicated. Patients with intrasellar germinomas have a favorable prognosis and long-term follow-up is important to detect relapse or progression of residual disease.

The patient was admitted to the hospital due to an eight-month history of generalized fatigue, increased thirst, increased urinary frequency and volume, reduced nocturnal erections, decreased sexual desire, weight loss of 18 kg in six months, dry skin, cold intolerance, and constipation. The initial laboratory examination revealed hypopituitarism, hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, polyuria, and hypertonic hypernatremia. The initial MRI scan showed a right-sided pituitary microadenoma. New laboratory examination results confirmed the previous findings and ruled out the presence of autoimmune or inflammatory conditions. Tumor markers for germ cell tumors were negative. records.source_note:
Hospital Course:

The patient, a 17-year-old female, was referred after 31 months of orthodontic treatment, with a history of surgical orthodontic traction resulting in an unfavorable outcome. The current anamneses and physical exam revealed an orthodontic device for space maintenance between teeth 12 and 14 and tooth 13 with clinical exposure of its crown on the palate and three orthodontic buttons present for elastic traction. Periapical and panoramic radiographic exams showed significant bone loss distal to 12 and mesial to 14, with tooth 13 apex constrained within the ennis inverted Y. 

After proper orthodontic treatment, the patient and parents were informed of the possible prosthetic rehabilitation alternatives and opted for partial maxillary osteotomy. The procedure, performed on March 02, 2001, comprised of the maxillary right canine removal and a partial maxillary osteotomy. 

Post-surgically, elastic traction was applied to conclude the approximation of the distal segment. Intermaxillary immobilization was sustained for 21 days, and during weekly postoperatory controls, the orthodontic arch-wire was substituted for a continuous arch to maintain stability of the segment and encourage the formation of a callus. 

Following the treatment, full orthodontic movements were cleared in April 24, 2001. Full treatment was concluded on October 23, 2001, and removable retainers were installed. The patient requested the removal of the internal rigid fixation on October 29, 2010. On the clinical and radiographic control of January 10 and 17, 2012, stability and pulpar vitality could be confirmed after 10 years and 10 months of follow-up with excellent periodontal conditions.

The patient, a 17-year-old female, was referred after 31 months of orthodontic treatment, with a history of surgical orthodontic traction resulting in an unfavorable outcome. The current anamneses and physical exam revealed an orthodontic device for space maintenance between teeth 12 and 14 and tooth 13 with clinical exposure of its crown on the palate and three orthodontic buttons present for elastic traction. Periapical and panoramic radiographic exams showed significant bone loss distal to 12 and mesial to 14, with tooth 13 apex constrained within the ennis inverted Y. 

After proper orthodontic treatment, the patient and parents were informed of the possible prosthetic rehabilitation alternatives and opted for partial maxillary osteotomy. The procedure, performed on March 02, 2001, comprised of the maxillary right canine removal and a partial maxillary osteotomy. 

Post-surgically, elastic traction was applied to conclude the approximation of the distal segment. Intermaxillary immobilization was sustained for 21 days, and during weekly postoperatory controls, the orthodontic arch-wire was substituted for a continuous arch to maintain stability of the segment and encourage the formation of a callus. 

Following the treatment, full orthodontic movements were cleared in April 24, 2001. Full treatment was concluded on October 23, 2001, and removable retainers were installed. The patient requested the removal of the internal rigid fixation on October 29, 2010. On the clinical and radiographic control of January 10 and 17, 2012, stability and pulpar vitality could be confirmed after 10 years and 10 months of follow-up with excellent periodontal conditions.

records.source_note:
Discharge Summary:

Patient Information:
Name: [REDACTED]
Age: 54
Sex: Female
Date of Admission: [REDACTED]
Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]
Admitting Diagnosis: Sodium hydroxide splash injury of left eye 
Final Diagnosis: Symblepharon with superficial and deep corneal neovascularization

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to our eye emergency department with light perception in the left eye and congested eyelids and conjunctiva caused by a splash injury of sodium hydroxide. A diffuse corneal epithelial defect, stromal edema, and localized Descemet’s folds were observed during the initial examination. The patient was treated with 1% dexamethasone sodium phosphate drops, 1% atropine drops, and tobramycin. She was then given prednisone 50mg, daily for ten days, followed by a gradual taper by 5mg every 15 days. Despite frequent use of topical steroids, the patient developed a symblepharon and superficial and deep corneal neovascularization after three months.

Treatment:
A subconjunctival bevacizumab injection of 0.05ml (1.25mg) was administered to the left eye with the aim of reducing corneal neovascularization. The patient was advised to use 0.3% ofloxacin and 1% dexamethasone sodium phosphate drops three times daily for one week after the subconjunctival bevacizumab injection. A second subconjunctival bevacizumab injection was given when the vessels began to perfuse again two weeks after the first injection.

Outcome:
The patient's visual acuity improved to 0.1 logarithm of the minimum angle of resolution (LogMAR) two weeks after the second injection, and the corneal neovascularization was significantly reduced. During the next months, the patient's condition was well-controlled, and at the end of follow-up 24 months later, her VA and clinical condition were unaltered.

1. Patient is a 51-year-old male diagnosed with stage intravenous pulmonary adenocarcinoma.
2. Patient presented with lymphadenopathy in the left neck, mediastinum, and a lung tubercle.
3. Received combination chemotherapy, nimotuzumab, maintenance pemetrexed, and autologous lymphocyte reinfusion.
4. Underwent mediastinal lymphadenectomy and wedge resection of the lower lobe of the right lung.
5. Postoperative pathology identified large cell carcinoma.
6. Metastasis was detected in the central nervous system.
7. Received three cycles of combination chemotherapy and whole brain radiation therapy.
8. Experienced joint swelling and pain, which improved after treatment.
9. Undergoing immunotherapy with pembrolizumab at 31 months post-initiation.
10. Discharge status is asymptomatic, 31 months post-pembrolizumab initiation.
records.source_note:
Discharge Summary:

Patient Information:
Name: [Redacted]
Gender: Male
Age: 51 years
Admission Date: [Redacted]
Discharge Date: N/A

Chief Complaint:
Lymphadenopathy in the left neck, mediastinum, and a tubercle in the right lung.

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 51-year-old heavy smoker, was admitted with lymphadenopathy in the left neck, mediastinum, and a tubercle in the right lung. Pathological examination of transbronchial needle aspiration biopsy specimens identified an adenocarcinoma, and the patient was diagnosed with stage IV pulmonary adenocarcinoma. After being treated with four cycles of combination chemotherapy, 11 cycles of nimotuzumab, 12 cycles of maintenance pemetrexed, and 38 cycles of autologous lymphocyte reinfusion, the patient underwent mediastinal lymphadenectomy and wedge resection of the lower lobe of the right lung by video-assisted thoracic surgery. The postoperative pathology indicated large cell carcinoma. Immunohistochemical analysis showed several markers. After surgery, the patient was administered three cycles of combination chemotherapy. Subsequently, metastasis was detected in his CNS, and he underwent whole brain radiation therapy. On the 15th month after initial pembrolizumab administration, the patient had joint swelling and pain, which improved after symptomatic treatment.

Hospital Course Summary:
-Admitted for lymphadenopathy in the left neck, mediastinum, and right lung tubercle 
-Diagnosed with stage IV pulmonary adenocarcinoma 
-Treated with combination chemotherapy, nimotuzumab, maintenance pemetrexed, and autologous lymphocyte reinfusion 
-Underwent mediastinal lymphadenectomy and wedge resection of the lower lobe of the right lung by video-assisted thoracic surgery 
-Administered three cycles of combination chemotherapy 
-Subsequently, metastasis to CNS detected 
-Underwent whole brain radiation therapy 
-Administered 18 cycles of pembrolizumab 
-Experienced joint swelling and pain, improved after treatment 

Diagnostic Tests and Procedures:
-Transbronchial needle aspiration biopsy 
-Endobronchial ultrasonography 
-Mediastinal lymphadenectomy 
-Wedge resection of the lower lobe of the right lung by video-assisted thoracic surgery 
-Immunohistochemical analysis 
-Gene detection 
-MRI 

Follow-Up Plan:
At the time of submission of this report, the patient continues on treatment and remains completely asymptomatic, 31 months after initiation of pembrolizumab. No further follow-up plan specified at this time.

N/A 

Discharge Medications:
N/A

DISCHARGE SUMMARY:

Patient Name: [REDACTED] 

Date of Admission: [REDACTED] 

Date of Discharge: [REDACTED] 

Admitting Diagnosis: Heart failure with renal artery aneurysm and arteriovenous fistula 

Principal Diagnosis at Discharge: Heart failure with renal artery aneurysm and arteriovenous fistula 

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted with complaints of dyspnea, lower extremity swelling, and abdominal distension. Physical examination revealed irregularly irregular rhythm, tender hepatomegaly, and bilateral lower extremity edema. Laboratory analysis showed elevated B-type Natriuretic Peptide (BNP) levels and transthoracic echocardiogram revealed right heart failure with dilated right atrium and ventricle.

Further evaluation with ultrasound and CT angiogram revealed a large renal artery aneurysm and arteriovenous fistula. The patient was deemed a poor surgical candidate and managed by endovascular occlusion. The aneurysm was completely obliterated using large coils and the feeding distal renal artery was occluded with Amplatzer vascular plug II.

Result:

Following endovascular occlusion, the patient's symptoms improved and the clinical exam showed resolution of jugular venous distention, decreased abdominal distension, and lower extremity edema. The ascites resolved on follow-up CT and BNP levels decreased at 6 months of follow-up.

Discharge Instructions:

The patient is advised to follow up with their primary care physician for further evaluation and management of heart failure and renal artery aneurysm. The patient should continue their medications and adhere to a low-salt diet. They are also advised to maintain a healthy lifestyle and avoid any activities that may cause undue stress or exertion.

records.source_note:
Discharge Summary:

Patient Information:
Name: Vietnamese, 55-year-old male
Diagnosis: HBV cirrhosis without HDV, HCV or HIV coinfections
Complication: Grade 1 oesophageal varices

Hospital Course:
The patient was diagnosed with HBV cirrhosis without HDV, HCV or HIV coinfections in 1997. The probable route of infection was vertical transmission. After diagnosis, liver biopsy was done to confirm cirrhosis. The patient's condition was complicated by Grade 1 oesophageal varices and scored A5 in Child Pugh.

In August 1998, the patient started taking lamivudine at 100 mg/day due to the rising levels of HBV-DNA and ALT values. After 3 months of medication, the patient's HBV-DNA levels were undetectable by Digene assay. In February 1999, the patient's HBV-DNA levels were undetectable by qualitative PCR that had a sensitivity limit at 4 log10.

In January 2000, lamivudine medication was inadvertently stopped after only ten months of treatment. The patient was diagnosed with a relapse after the rising levels of HBV-DNA to 5.75 log10, ALT values at 3.1 ULN. The treatment continued for the next two years, where HBV-DNA was undetectable by quantitative PCR (cut-off at 2.3 log10, MONITOR COBAS, Roche), and ALT values were within the normal range.

In January 2002, HBV-DNA became detectable by PCR, and then, in June 2002, a viral breakthrough was documented with HBV-DNA levels at 9.2 log10 and ALT at 2.7 ULN. The patient was found to be asymptomatic. Upon sequencing of the HBV polymerase, two common lamivudine resistant mutations – rtL180M and rtM204V – were detected. To the ongoing lamivudine treatment, adefovir dipivoxil, 10 mg/day, was added; however, the following 10 months of treatment were uneventful, and HBV-DNA levels never fell below 5 log10. In June 2003, the HBV-DNA titer was 5.28 log10, and lamivudine medication was stopped, but adefovir was maintained; in addition, pegylated interferon α-2a was used as additional treatment. After five injections, the patient stopped pegylated interferon administration because of poor drug tolerance: anorexia, dry mouth, diarrhea, weight loss, and back pain. Thrombopenia was also detected.

After four months of uninterrupted adefovir monotherapy, HBV-DNA was still at 4.9 log10 and the same lamivudine resistant mutations were detected without adefovir resistant mutations. In September 2004, while on adefovir monotherapy, and 15 months after having stopped lamivudine and 13 months after having stopped pegylated interferon, HBV-DNA rose to 8.3 log10, ALT to 10 ULN and aspartate aminotransferase to 7 ULN. Prothrombin time was 78%, and total bilirubin and serum albumin were normal. Two adefovir resistant mutations, rtA181T and rtN236T, were detected.

The patient was then given a test trial of higher doses of adefovir (20 mg/day). However, after a month, HBV-DNA reached 7 log10 levels, ALT levels remained unchanged, and the patient's condition continued to deteriorate. The patient developed oedema, ascites, jaundice, mild renal insufficiency (serum creatinine 110 μmol/l), and a decreased prothrombin time (47% of normal). Therefore, tenofovir fumarate was started at a dose of 300 mg/day, while adefovir was continued for one month, and then it was stopped.

Two months later, HBV-DNA became undetectable by PCR, and the patient's prothrombin time level rose to 90%. The patient's jaundice and ascites also resolved. After eight months of tenofovir treatment, the patient's HBV-DNA was still undetectable by PCR on three separate occasions as of the most recent testing. 

Overall, the patient's condition remained unremarkable during the hospital stay. The patient is currently listed for liver transplantation as the treatment of HBV cirrhosis.

records.source_note:
DISCHARGE SUMMARY

Patient Name: [REDACTED]    Gender: Male    Date of Admission: [REDACTED]    Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]

HOSPITAL COURSE:
2-day old male newborn was referred to us because of distended abdomen, abnormal genitalia and imperforate anus. Examination of genitalia revealed a well-formed double penis with normally located and functioning urethra, left penis had proximal hypospadias. There were normal penile shaft and bifid scrotum with each compartment containing a testicle. Perineal examination showed imperforate anus. The values of blood analysis were within normal ranges. Abdominal sonography showed distended bowel loops and bilateral normal kidneys. The patient underwent laparotomy and colostomy the day after admission, the colon was distended and duplicated.

Two months later, an intravenous pyelography was performed which showed normal kidneys and ureters. Voiding-cystourethrography revealed double bladder and urethra, but no vesicourethral reflux. At 4 months of age, surgical exploration of genitourinary tract showed the abnormal position of bladder and urethra. Cystoplasty and reimplantation of left ureter into a single bladder were performed. Left-side urethra with hypospadias was resected, and bifid scrotum repaired. Post-operative days passed without complication so that the patient could be discharged 2 weeks later.

At the age of one year, after colostogram and total colon evaluation, laparotomy, resection of duplicated recto-sigmoid colon and pull-through, and 3 months later colostomy closure was carried out. The patient was under observation until the age of 4 years when his parents decided to leave Iran due to family problems.

DISCHARGE DIAGNOSIS:
Abnormal Genitalia with Double Penis and Hypospadias, Imperforate Anus with Distended and Duplicated Bowel Loops, Duplicated Recto-Sigmoid Colon

DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS:
Parents should schedule regular follow-up appointments with their primary care physician for monitoring and management of the patient's condition. They should also discuss any further diagnostic or treatment options with their healthcare provider if necessary. It is essential to follow a healthy diet and hygiene practices to prevent complications and discomfort.

SUMMARY:
The patient, a 2-day old male newborn, was referred to us due to abnormal genitalia and imperforate anus. He underwent laparotomy and colostomy, cystoplasty, and surgical exploration, which led to a diagnosis of Abnormal Genitalia with Double Penis and Hypospadias, Imperforate Anus with Distended and Duplicated Bowel Loops, and Duplicated Recto-Sigmoid Colon. The patient was successfully treated, and after a series of follow-up interventions, he was discharged with instructions for regular care follow-up.

Cystoplasty and reimplantation of left ureter into a single bladder were performed. Left-side urethra with hypospadias was resected, and bifid scrotum repaired. Post-operative days passed without complication so that the patient could be discharged 2 weeks later.

At the age of one year, after colostogram and total colon evaluation, laparotomy, resection of duplicated recto-sigmoid colon and pull-through, and 3 months later colostomy closure was carried out. The patient was under observation until the age of 4 years when his parents decided to leave Iran due to family problems.

Discharge Summary

Patient Name: [Name]
Sex: Female
Age: 40
Reason for Admission: Infertility Treatment

Hospital Course:

The patient was a 40-year-old woman who entered the hospital for infertility treatment and underwent a laparoscopic-assisted myomectomy. Timed intercourse was initiated three months after the surgery. The patient was diagnosed with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) based on an irregular cycle and high anti-Mullerian hormone (AMH) levels. Standard treatment guidelines in Japan were followed, and the patient underwent timed intercourse with cyclofenil administered at a dose of 600 mg/d for 5 days, starting on cycle day 5 until cycle day 9. However, no follicular development was observed even on the 25th day of the menstrual cycle. The patient received 4 mg/d of chlormadinone acetate for 10 days, followed by timed intercourse with clomiphene citrate, which was administered at a dose of 50 mg/day for 5 days starting on cycle day 5 until cycle day 9. We observed a 48 × 41 mm anechoic mass in the patient's right ovary on the ultrasonogram on the 11th day of the menstrual cycle, which we initially considered a follicle and monitored its progress. Subsequent mass sizes on days 16th, 20th, 21st, and 28th mentioned the gradual change in the mass configuration. The mass disappeared on the 62nd day since detection (19th day of the menstrual cycle), and we diagnosed the mass as a HOC according to its clinical course.

Hospital Course Summary:

The 40-year-old female patient with a history of ureteral stones, Behcet's disease, and multiple myoma underwent a laparoscopic-assisted myomectomy for infertility treatment at our hospital. After the surgery, timed intercourse was initiated, and a diagnosis of PCOS was made based on an irregular cycle and high AMH levels. Treatment guidelines were followed, with the patient receiving medication to increase the chances of successful ovulation. A 48 × 41 mm anechoic mass was observed in the patient's right ovary, which was initially considered a follicle, but its course indicated it to be a HOC. The patient showed no symptoms, was closely monitored, and received follow-up without any medication for infertility treatment. The patient was discharged in good health, and further follow-up will be done during her next routine visit.

records.source_note:
DISCHARGE SUMMARY

Admitting Diagnosis: Paradoxical Reaction
 
Hospital Course:
The patient was referred to the department due to the appearance of a new mass on chest CT during a regular routine checkup. Past medical history included undergoing anti-tuberculosis therapy for six months for a 1.7×1.4cm nodule in the right-superior pulmonary lobe. Induction chemotherapy was initiated with isoniazid, rifampicin, ethambutol, pyrazinamide and levofloxacin, which were later changed to isoniazid, rifapentine and ethambutol due to liver damage. Symptoms of the patient were gradually improving. However, one week before this admission, CT scans revealed a new occupying lesion in the right-inferior lobe. CT-guided percutaneous lung biopsy demonstrated caseating granulomas, confirming the diagnosis of paradoxical reaction. The patient was continued on anti-tuberculosis therapy, and the size of the new pulmonary mass was reduced. The patient is asymptomatic, and the original therapy still continues.

Patient Information:
Name: [Name]
Age: 70
Sex: Female
Medical Record Number: [Number]

Admission Information:
Date of Admission: [Date]
Reason for Admission: Changes to skin of left breast

Hospital Course:
The patient presented to the outpatient breast clinic after noticing changes to the skin of her left breast. She first noticed skin discoloration 6 months earlier, which had grown continuously causing her to seek treatment. The patient had a medical history significant for hypertension, high cholesterol, diabetes mellitus, and osteoporosis, but no prior breast health issues or surgeries. The patient denied any associated symptoms, including pain, new masses, nipple discharge/retraction, or lymphadenopathy. On physical exam, vital signs were all within normal limits and the patient had no obvious signs of distress. Breast examination was normal apart from a single 3 × 3 cm pink, non-tender, raised lesion of the left breast at the 12:00 position. After discussing possible treatment options the patient agreed to an excisional biopsy. She tolerated this procedure well without complication.

Diagnosis:
Based on pathology results, the patient was diagnosed with primary cutaneous ALCL.

Treatment:
Given the lack of invasion and negative margins, it was recommended that no further treatment be given. The patient is recovering well and is being managed through active surveillance.

Follow-up:
The patient was referred to oncology for follow-up.

Discharge Information:
Date of Discharge: [Date]
Discharge Diagnosis: Primary cutaneous ALCL

Instructions:
The patient is to follow-up with oncology as directed.

Signed,
[Physician Name], MD

Discharge Summary:

Patient name: [Patient's name]

Discharge date: [Discharge date]

Admission date: [Admission date]

Admitting diagnosis: RVOT-VT with chest pain and palpitations 

Hospital course: 

The patient, a 70-year-old male with multiple comorbidities, presented to the emergency department with chest pain and palpitations. Initial evaluation showed the presence of right ventricular outflow tract ventricular tachycardia (RVOT-VT) which was managed with external cardioversion. Subsequently, the patient was started on intravenous amiodarone and underwent further evaluation that revealed left ventricular systolic dysfunction with a double chamber in the right ventricle. The patient was diagnosed with obstructive coronary artery disease several years ago, which was not treated. He had a brief episode of recurrent RVOT-VT, which was managed with another amiodarone loading dose. Subsequently, surgical options including resection of the muscular band, coronary artery bypass grafting and subcutaneous ICD placement were explored. The patient refused surgical options and was discharged home with only a subcutaneous ICD in place.

Discharge medications: 

The patient was discharged on his prior medication regimen including aspirin, atorvastatin, digoxin, lisinopril and spironolactone-hydrochlorothiazide. 

Follow-up appointments: 

The patient was advised to follow up with his primary care physician and specialists as needed. 

Primary care physician: [Name of the primary care physician]

Specialists: [List of specialist physicians] 

Discharge condition: 

The patient was discharged in stable condition. He was able to ambulate independently and was advised to follow up with his healthcare providers as needed. 

Discharge instructions: 

The patient was instructed to continue the prescribed medications as directed, and to monitor his symptoms and report any changes to his healthcare providers. He was also advised to follow up with his healthcare providers as scheduled and to seek immediate medical attention if he experienced any worsening of symptoms or new symptoms.

records.submitted_statements:
1. The patient is a 22-year-old female of Indian origin presenting with lip swelling and recurrent angular cheilitis.
2. Laboratory findings revealed microcytic hypochromic anemia with low serum iron and folate levels.
3. Blood tests also showed an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate.
4. Hematological tests remained stable over a 15-month follow-up period.
5. Biopsy results excluded intestinal involvement of Crohn's disease.
6. Mantoux and Kveim tests were negative for active tuberculosis and sarcoidosis.
7. Treatment included anti-inflammatory medications, corticosteroids, topical steroids, and vitamin supplements.
8. External gingivectomy was considered after oral prophylaxis.
9. No gastrointestinal symptoms were reported during follow-up.
10. Oral ulcerations and lip swelling improved with treatment, but gingival normalization was not achieved.
records.source_note:
Hospital Course:
The 22-year-old female of Indian origin was referred to the Department of Periodontics due to persistent lip swelling and recurrent episodes of angular cheilitis. Hematological examination was consistent with microcytic hypochromic anemia, and further blood investigations showed low serum iron and folate levels, and raised erythrocyte sedimentation rate. The patient did not report any gastrointestinal disturbances, but a biopsy was performed to rule out intestinal involvement. Mantoux and Kveim tests ruled out active tubercular infection and sarcoidosis. 

Diagnosis:
Based on clinical findings, histopathologic examination, and laboratory investigations, the patient was diagnosed with oral Crohn's disease without intestinal manifestations. 

Treatment:
Anti-inflammatory drugs and corticosteroid supplements were prescribed and topical steroid applications were advised to relieve oral ulcerations. Hydrocortisone ointment and vitamin supplements were recommended to treat angular cheilitis. External gingivectomy was planned after extensive oral prophylaxis and subgingival scaling. 

Follow-up:
The patient was followed up for 15 months, during which there were no gastrointestinal symptoms. Repeat hematological tests showed no marked variation from the initial findings. Although oral ulcerations and lip swelling responded to treatment, normal appearance of the gingiva was not achieved. 

Conclusion:
In conclusion, the 22-year-old female of Indian origin was diagnosed with oral Crohn's disease without intestinal manifestations. She was treated with a combination of anti-inflammatory drugs and corticosteroid supplements. The patient showed improvement in oral ulcerations and lip swelling but did not achieve a complete recovery.

records.source_note:
Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]

Date of Admission: [REDACTED]

Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted to the hospital with difficulty flushing the PEG tube and localized PEG-tube site pain. During the physical exam, an external bulge was noted at the gastrostomy site, and there appeared to be external migration of the PEG tube. After considering these findings, BBS was suspected. 

An esophagogastroduodenoscopy was conducted to explore the issue. During the test, a bulge was discovered at the fistula site. The internal bumper embedded within the fistula tract was identified but maintained within the gastric lumen. 

Following an external traction, the buried PEG tube was removed without complications. Finally, a 14 F, 1.7-cm Mic-Key® button (Halyard Health, Alpharetta, GA, USA) was placed over the guidewire successfully. Kidney, ureter, and bladder X-ray (KUB) was conducted, which showed no free air. Later, the patient was discharged home without complications. 

Diagnosis:

The patient was diagnosed with difficulty flushing the PEG tube and localized PEG-tube site pain.

Treatment:

The treatment involved external traction, PEG tube removal, and placement of a 14 F, 1.7-cm Mic-Key® button over the guidewire successfully. 

Follow-up:

On discharge, the patient did not require further hospital follow-up.

Discharge Medications:

No medications were prescribed at the discharge.

Discharge Condition:

The patient was discharged in a stable condition without complications.

records.source_note:
Hospital Course:

The 6-year-old female patient was admitted for evaluation of a left-sided diagnosis of CMT and an incidental finding of a right-sided chest wall mass that was detected during assessment of a persistent dry cough. No predisposing factors were identified.

Physical Exam:

The patient exhibited left-sided torticollis and a firm, nontender mass of size 6 cm × 4 cm, with fixation to the posterior chest wall at the level of the fourth-sixth ribs on the right side. A chest skiagram revealed a mass arising from the right upper chest wall, leading to the collapse of the right upper zone. Subsequent computed tomography of the chest confirmed a destructive osseous lesion that involved the right fourth, fifth, and sixth ribs posteriorly.

Management:

A right posterolateral thoracotomy was performed in conjunction with excision of the tumor and release of the left sternocleidomastoid (SCM) tendon . Histopathology revealed the presence of dense hyalinized fibrocollagenous tissue with bone and focal pseudocartilaginous areas without evidence of epidermal or smooth muscle differentiation. Additionally, the tumor margin was negative. Based on these findings, our diagnosis was a desmoid tumor.

Discharge Summary:

The 6-year-old female patient with CMT and an incidentally detected right-sided chest wall mass underwent a right posterolateral thoracotomy with excision of the tumor, freeing of the left SCM tendon, and partial removal of the fifth rib. Pathology revealed a desmoid tumor with negative margins. The patient is to be closely monitored for potential future recurrences, follow-up will be conducted by oncology.

Medications: None

Follow-up: Oncology

Conditions on discharge: Desmoid tumor

Discharge Summary

Patient Name: [MP]

Medical Record #: [insert number]

Date of Admission: [insert date]

Date of Discharge: [insert date]

Admitting Diagnosis: Chronic pain syndrome with failed back surgery syndrome (FBSS)

Hospital Course: 

The patient presented with a long-standing history of intractable chronic pain predominantly in the lower back and both legs despite multiple surgical and non-surgical interventions, including 14 spinal surgeries, block injections, and medications. The patient was found to have a mixed pain syndrome composed of a neuropathic radicular component in both legs plus a nociceptive component in the lower back secondary to FBSS. The initial treatment with spinal cord stimulation (SCS) achieved excellent bilateral pain relief for the legs but not for the axial lower back pain. The patient subsequently underwent deep brain stimulation (DBS) of the periaqueductal gray (PVG) on the nondominant side, and achieved excellent axial spinal pain relief. 

During the 22 years of follow-up, whenever both SCS and DBS neuromodulation systems were operating and utilized simultaneously, complete relief of back and leg pain has been maintained. However, electrode programming adjustments have been carried out as necessary, such as after accidental exposure to magnetic fields or after generator battery depletion. In addition, wire-connector revisions were twice required after motor vehicle accidents. The patient's chronic pain condition has been completely controlled with the neuromodulation intervention for the past 22 years. He has been able to return to living a normal life without interference by chronic pain in his activities. 

Discharge Diagnosis: Chronic pain syndrome with FBSS, controlled with combined SCS/PVG-stimulation.

Treatment: Neuromodulation intervention with SCS and DBS.

Condition at Discharge: Stable, pain-free.

Follow-Up Care: The patient will continue to follow up with the neurosurgical pain clinic for regular reprogramming visits and maintenance of the neuromodulation systems. 

Signed,

[insert name of physician]

2. He has a history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, diabetes mellitus type 2, high cholesterol, and alcohol abuse.
3. Physical examination findings include petechiae, hematoma, elevated white blood cell count, and signs of leukostasis.
4. Laboratory results showed a very high white blood cell count (220 × 10⁹/l), low hemoglobin, and dangerously low platelets.
5. Peripheral blood smear revealed a high number of blasts and promyelocytes consistent with acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL).
6. Elevated lactate dehydrogenase and creatinine were noted.
7. Coagulation studies were normal.
8. Treatment included leukapheresis, chemotherapy, and ATRA.
9. The patient's condition improved following the intervention.
10. He was discharged with appropriate post-treatment instructions.
records.source_note:
Hospital Course:

The 76-year-old man presented with exertional dyspnea, visual disturbances, night sweats and progressive fatigue. His medical history showed chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, Diabetes Mellitus type 2, high cholesterol and alcohol abuse. On physical examination, he had some petechiae and hematoma on the lower extremities. No lymphadenopathy or organomegaly was found. His white blood cell count was extremely elevated (220 × 109/l). Hemoglobin was low and platelets were dangerously low. The peripheral blood smear revealed a large number of blasts, but also a significant amount of promyelocytes, resembling typical APL. Other abnormal laboratory findings included high levels of LDH and creatinine. No coagulation abnormalities were present.

Treatment:

Due to signs of leukostasis, the patient was immediately treated with leukapheresis in addition to the administration of chemotherapy and ATRA. 

Conclusion:

Based on the diagnostic and treatment plan, the patient's condition improved and he was discharged with proper instructions for continued care.

records.source_note:
Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]

Date of Admission: [REDACTED]

Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]

Diagnosis:
- Poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma with squamous features suggestive of pancreaticobiliary primary.

Hospital Course:
- The patient was admitted to the hospital with complaints of generalized body weakness, difficulty sleeping, abdominal pain, increased thirst with urinary frequency, and constipation.
- Physical examination revealed normal vital signs except for hepatomegaly.
- Laboratory evaluation showed leukocytosis, elevated corrected calcium levels, elevated alkaline phosphatase levels, normal phosphorus levels, low vitamin D levels, high PTHrP levels, and normal kidney function.
- CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis with intravenous contrast revealed a large complex appearing mass within the liver appearing as multifocal lesions with a large central hypodense lesion and numerous peripheral satellite lesions.
- PET-CT reported extensive hyper-metabolic activity in the liver, consistent with malignancy. It revealed hypermetabolic abdominal lymph nodes, mildly hypermetabolic activity in the omentum/peritoneum, and ascites.
- CT-guided biopsy of the liver was performed, and pathology showed poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma with squamous features supportive of pancreaticobiliary as primary.
- Chemotherapy with cisplatin and gemcitabine was started after the diagnosis was confirmed.
- The patient had recurrent admissions with worsening symptoms and uncontrolled hypercalcemia.
- His course was also complicated further with acute kidney injury, cholestatic hyperbilirubinemia, and pancreatitis and required placement of percutaneous transhepatic cholecystostomy (PTC).
- The patient’s condition further deteriorated, and he expired within three months of his diagnosis.

Discharge Summary:

Patient: Case 8, 30-year-old female

Chief Complaint: Elevated CK, episodes of palpitation

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted for further evaluation of her elevated creatine kinase (CK) levels and episodes of palpitation. The initial workup revealed a T wave inversion on electrocardiogram (ECG) and a normal transthoracic echocardiography (TTE). Further genetic testing utilizing next-generation sequencing based testing for a muscular dystrophy (MD) gene panel revealed a heterozygous carrier status for a missense variant of unknown significance (VUS) in the COL6A1 gene (c. 1273-4T>C). 

The patient was monitored overnight and remained stable. Consultation with the cardiology team recommended outpatient follow-up with ECG monitoring, Holter monitoring, and possible exercise stress testing. The patient was discharged with follow-up instructions.

Follow-up Instructions:

The patient was advised to continue her medications for systemic lupus erythematosus and to follow-up with her primary care physician for further workup of her elevated CK levels. The patient was also advised to schedule an appointment with cardiology for further monitoring of her palpitation episodes. Genetic counseling was recommended to discuss the significance of the VUS variant in COL6A1 gene.

Follow-up with orthopedics was also recommended for further evaluation of the patient's myalgia symptoms. 

The patient was discharged in stable condition with instructions to follow-up with her healthcare providers.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [Redacted]
Date of Admission: [Redacted]
Date of Discharge: [Redacted]

Brief Hospital Course:
The patient, a 29-year-old female medical microbiologist in training, was admitted to our hospital on [Redacted] with symptoms of low grade fever, general malaise and a retro-orbital headache related to eye movements, which she developed three days after returning from Suriname. The patient reported having been bitten by mosquitos during her visit to Paramaribo, the Brokopondo Lake and the Commewijne district. Three days after onset of initial symptoms, the patient developed a non-itching maculopapular rash on her trunk and extremities and slight conjunctival injection and redness in her face. The patient also experienced stiffness and edematous swelling of her wrists, knees and ankles. Throughout the course of disease she had contact lens intolerance. However, her symptoms did not lead to lost working days and her condition improved and symptoms diminished after 7 days.

Diagnostic Assessment:
On the fifth day of her illness, the patient visited our outpatient clinic where urine and blood was collected for diagnosis and characterization of an arboviral infection. Urine and plasma tested positive for ZIKV RNA by an in-house qRT-PCR (manuscript in preparation), and the plasma also tested positive in virus culture. No infectious virus could be recovered from the urine.

Summary of Events:
The patient was diagnosed with ZIKV infection after returning from a trip to Suriname where she had been bitten by mosquitos. She presented with low grade fever, general malaise and a retro-orbital headache related to eye movements, followed by a non-itching maculopapular rash on her trunk and extremities and slight conjunctival injection, which she recorded on photo, stiffness and edematous swelling of her wrists, knees and ankles and contact lens intolerance. She remained symptomatically stable throughout her stay and was discharged after 7 days of observation. 

Follow-Up:
Instructions were given to the patient and to seek medical attention if any future concerns related to her condition develop. Further management was deferred. 

Discharged home in stable condition.

Diagnostic assessment results include positive ZIKV RNA in urine and plasma by in-house qRT-PCR and positive virus culture in plasma. However, further management was deferred and instructions given to the patient to seek medical attention if any future concerns related to her condition develop.

1. Patient is a 62-year-old male with a history of tobacco abuse diagnosed with small-cell lung cancer.
2. Patient presented with shortness of breath and jugular venous distension following chemotherapy and radiation.
3. History of acute idiopathic pericarditis diagnosed four days prior.
4. Admission laboratory findings included hypoxemia, elevated creatinine, elevated lactate, and marked jugular venous distension.
5. ECG showed diffuse ST-segment elevations; echocardiography revealed large pericardial effusion causing tamponade.
6. Pericardiocentesis was performed and 800 mL of fluid drained.
7. Diagnosed with purulent pericarditis treated with ertapenem.
8. Performed partial pericardiectomy; sepsis resolved.
9. Pericardial effusion recurrence did not occur four weeks post-discharge.
10. Resumed chemotherapy and radiation therapy two months after discharge.
records.source_note:
Discharge Summary:
Patient Name: [Patient Name]
MR#: [Medical Record Number]

Hospitals Course:
The patient, a 62-year-old male with a history of tobacco abuse and newly diagnosed small-cell lung cancer, was readmitted to the hospital with shortness of breath. He had been on chemotherapy and radiation for his lung cancer over the course of the previous month. Four days prior to this admission, he was diagnosed with acute idiopathic pericarditis for which he was started on medication. 

Admission Findings:
Upon this admission, the patient had a temperature and was slightly hypoxic. During the physical examination, he was found to have marked jugular venous distension without Kussmaul's sign and pulsus paradoxus. Lab results showed significant abnormalities, including reduced white blood cell and neutrophil counts, elevated creatinine and blood urea nitrogen levels, and high lactic acid levels. An electrocardiogram showed normal voltage with diffuse ST-segment elevations. Urgent transthoracic echocardiography revealed large pericardial effusion causing tamponade physiology and right ventricular collapse in diastole and dilated inferior vena cava. Emergency pericardiocentesis was performed, and 800 mL of green fluid was drained.

Treatment and Outcome:
The patient was diagnosed with purulent pericarditis, and antibiotics were tailored to intravenous ertapenem based on microbial cultures from the pericardial fluid. He underwent partial pericardiectomy and sepsis resolved. The source of the polymicrobial pericarditis was unclear despite an extensive work-up including a computed tomography scan of the abdomen and the chest. The patient was discharged home on the eighth day of hospitalization. There was no recurrence of pericardial effusion according to the TTE 4 weeks following discharge. The patient eventually resumed chemo-radiation therapy 2 months after hospital discharge.

There was no recurrence of pericardial effusion according to the TTE four weeks following discharge. However, the source of the polymicrobial pericarditis was unclear despite extensive work-up including a computed tomography scan of the abdomen and the chest.

Discharge Summary:
Patient Name: [Patient Name]
MR#: [Medical Record Number]

Hospitals Course:
The patient, a 62-year-old male with a history of tobacco abuse and newly diagnosed small-cell lung cancer, was readmitted to the hospital with shortness of breath. He had been on chemotherapy and radiation for his lung cancer over the course of the previous month. Four days prior to this admission, he was diagnosed with acute idiopathic pericarditis for which he was started on medication. 

Admission Findings:
Upon this admission, the patient had a temperature and was slightly hypoxic. During the physical examination, he was found to have marked jugular venous distension without Kussmaul's sign and pulsus paradoxus. Lab results showed significant abnormalities, including reduced white blood cell and neutrophil counts, elevated creatinine and blood urea nitrogen levels, and high lactic acid levels. An electrocardiogram showed normal voltage with diffuse ST-segment elevations. Urgent transthoracic echocardiography revealed large pericardial effusion causing tamponade physiology and right ventricular collapse in diastole and dilated inferior vena cava. Emergency pericardiocentesis was performed, and 800 mL of green fluid was drained.

Treatment and Outcome:
The patient was diagnosed with purulent pericarditis, and antibiotics were tailored to intravenous ertapenem based on microbial cultures from the pericardial fluid. He underwent partial pericardiectomy and sepsis resolved. The source of the polymicrobial pericarditis was unclear despite an extensive work-up including a computed tomography scan of the abdomen and the chest. The patient was discharged home on the eighth day of hospitalization. There was no recurrence of pericardial effusion according to the TTE 4 weeks following discharge. The patient eventually resumed chemo-radiation therapy 2 months after hospital discharge.

The patient was admitted with a diagnosis of invasive low-grade carcinoma of the appendix colonizing appendicial endometriosis.

A 45-year-old female was admitted to the hospital for a second look laparotomy and HIPEC following a previous diagnosis of acute appendicitis, along with multiple peritoneal mucinous implants in the right pelvis.

The patient underwent right hemicolectomy, resection of two segments of small intestine, omentectomy, bilateral ovariectomy, and peritoneal resections with HIPEC administration. Invasive low-grade carcinoma of the appendix colonizing appendicial endometriosis.

The patient underwent right hemicolectomy, resection of two segments of small intestine, omentectomy, bilateral ovariectomy, and peritoneal resections with HIPEC administration.

Stable condition.

Close outpatient follow-up is recommended.

Hospital Course:

HOSPITAL COURSE SUMMARY:

Admission Date: [DATE]
Discharge Date: [DATE]

Patient Name: [PATIENT NAME]
Age: 74
Gender: Male

Diagnosis on Admission:
- Chronic bronchitis 
- Bronchial anthracofibrosis
- Right middle lobe atelectasis

Admission Notes:
The patient was admitted to the hospital due to repeated cough, expectoration, and wheezing for 8 years. Chest pain and shortness of breath were observed for 7 days. The patient was previously diagnosed with chronic bronchitis. Bronchoscopy showed obstruction in the right middle lobe. Acid-fast bacilli were negative on brush biopsy smear. Chest X-ray revealed right middle lobe atelectasis. The initial diagnosis was acute attack of chronic bronchitis and bronchial anthracofibrosis in the right middle lobe. The patient's symptoms were relieved after treatment of an exacerbation and was discharged from the hospital.

Hospital Course:
The patient presented to the hospital again due to chest pain and progressive shortness of breath 9 months from the initial diagnosis. Physical examination showed dullness to percussion in the right lung and the right lower lung breath sounds disappeared. Chest CT revealed right pleural effusion. Multiple white nodules of various sizes were seen on the parietal pleura. Biopsy was performed. Acid-fast bacilli were negative. Pleural effusion carcinoembryonic antigen was 1.37 ng/mL. Biopsy of pleura showed granulomatous inflammation of right parietal pleura. The diagnosis was revised to tuberculous pleuritis. After anti-tuberculosis treatment, the pleural effusion reduced remarkably, and the chest pain and shortness of breath were relieved. The pleural effusion disappeared 2 months after the end of anti-tuberculosis treatment, consistent with the diagnosis of tuberculous pleuritis.

Discharge Condition:
The patient was in stable condition upon discharge.

Outpatient Follow-up:
The patient was advised to follow up with the primary care physician regularly and continue anti-tuberculosis treatment as prescribed. The patient was also advised to maintain a healthy lifestyle to improve overall health and prevent recurrence of the disease.

Summary:
The patient presented with repeated cough, expectoration, and wheezing for 8 years. The initial diagnosis was chronic bronchitis and bronchial anthracofibrosis in the right middle lobe. However, due to the aggravation of symptoms and further testing, the diagnosis was revised to tuberculous pleuritis. The patient responded well to the prescribed anti-tuberculosis treatment. The patient was discharged in stable condition with outpatient follow-up advised.

The patient's medications will be adjusted and prescribed by the primary care provider.

Hospital Course Summary:

Admission Date: [insert date]
Discharge Date: [insert date]

Admission Diagnosis:
Decayed teeth with generalized gingivitis and multiple moderate-to-advanced dental caries in a 36-year-old male patient with Wilson's disease.

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to the dental hospital for operative, periodontal, and prosthodontic treatments. Due to his mental retardation and extreme fear and anxiety towards dental treatment, the procedures were performed under general anesthesia in two minimal visits. Throughout the procedures, his electrocardiography, heart rate, blood pressure, respiratory rate, end-tidal capnography, body temperature, and entropy levels were monitored. An IV line was secured under O2 and N2O gases, and 4% sevoflurane gas and atracurium were administered. The patient was then intubated with a 26-mm ETT under an adequate depth of anesthesia. Anesthesia was maintained with O2 and N2O gases and 2% sevoflurane. During both general anesthesia, the response entropy (RE) was maintained in the range of 35–54 and state entropy (SE) of 30–45. No specific events occurred during the procedures.

The patient received various operative, periodontal, and prosthodontic treatments, including scaling, composite filling, inlay preparation, gold crown preparation, simple extraction, and treatment of caries. During the try-in step, the gold crown for tooth 36 slid from the surgeon's hand and was incidentally found near the endotracheal tube balloon. The prosthesis was promptly removed using video-assisted laryngoscopy and curvilinear forceps. Dental floss-tied gauze packing was performed to prevent recurrence of the accident. The patient exhibited no specific complications during the procedure and was discharged 1 hour after stabilization.

Discharge Diagnosis:
Decayed teeth with generalized gingivitis and multiple moderate-to-advanced dental caries in a 36-year-old male patient with Wilson's disease.

Discharge Condition:
Stable with no complications.

Discharge Plan:
The patient is instructed to maintain routine medication and follow-up with his primary care physician. He is advised to maintain good oral hygiene and attend regular dental check-ups. The patient was provided with detailed postoperative instructions, including guidelines for incision care, activity, diet, and medication use. The patient and his guardian were fully informed of all aspects of his discharge and the need to seek immediate medical attention if necessary.

Discharge Medications:
None.

Follow-up Appointments:
Follow-up appointments with the primary care physician and regular dental check-ups are recommended.

records.source_note:
Hospital Course:

The patient is a 60-year-old female who presented to the emergency room with shortness of breath, palpitation, chest pain, and progressive dyspnea. She had a history of dyspnea on exertion and orthopnea too. Physical examination revealed arterial blood pressure of 135/90 mmHg, heart rate of 110 beats per minute, SpO2 94% on room air and respiratory rate of 24 breaths per minute. No significant medical history was noted.

Diagnostic Testing:

Cardiac enzymes, biochemical analysis, and complete blood count were normal except for eosinophilia. Chest radiography findings include cardiomegaly with bulging left heart boarder. Electrocardiography (ECG) showed normal sinus rhythm with poor progression of R wave in lead v4, v5, and v6 and no changes in ST segment. Transthoracic echocardiographic investigation showed a large multicystic mass seen intrapericardially extending from the left ventricle lateral wall to the pericardial sac causing pressure effect on left ventricle. Contrast-enhanced CT confirmed the presence of a well-defined, thin-walled, homogeneous multiple cardiac hydatid cyst with internal trabeculae arising from pericardium with adjacent structure. A serologic test for hydatidosis was positive for E. granulosus and marked eosinophilia was present too.

Treatment:

After diagnosis, the patient underwent surgery to remove the cyst. The cyst was successfully excised and pathology examination of the specimen was shown with hydatid cyst. Postoperative pain was managed with intercostal block with 0.5% of bupivacain plain, inj. tramadol, and diclofenac sodium I.M. The patient was extubated and had a normal hemodynamic status maintained intraoperatively and postoperatively.

Follow-up:

The patient's recovery was uneventful, and she did not experience any complications throughout her hospital stay. She was discharged with no restrictions and was advised to follow up with her physician for further management.

The patient had an uneventful recovery and was discharged with no restrictions with a recommendation for further follow-up with her physician.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY

Patient Name: Not provided            
Date of Admission: Not provided          
Date of Discharge: Not provided      

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 17-year-old Saudi male with a known history of bronchial asthma, was admitted to the emergency department with shortness of breath, nonproductive cough and wheezing for the last 48 hours. The patient had twice been hospitalized in the past 2 years due to a worsening of these symptoms. Upon examination, the patient was conscious but dyspneic. Vitals showed PR- 104/ min, RR- 28/min, BP- 104/68 mm Hg, SPO2-89% in normal room air by pulse oxymetry and 92% with 4 L/ min oxygen delivered through nasal canula. Extensive subcutaneous emphysema involving bilateral upper chest, neck and axillary regions was observed and a systolic crunching sound over the left parasternal region was present. The initial chest x-ray revealed surgical emphysema, pneumonic consolidation involving the right lower lobe, and air in the mediastinum and pericardium. Further testing via computed tomography (CT) revealed air dissection into subcutaneous, mediastinal, and pericardial spaces, as well as air in the posterior spinal epidural space at multiple cervical and thoracic levels.

The patient was treated with broad-spectrum antibiotics, inhalation bronchodilators, systemic corticosteroids, high-flow oxygen, and other supportive measures. The hospital stay was uneventful, and the patient showed a progressive improvement in his condition. He was subsequently shifted to cardiothoracic care. At the two-month follow-up, the patient was asymptomatic.

Diagnosis: 
Bronchial asthma, pneumonic consolidation involving the right lower lobe, surgical emphysema, subcutaneous emphysema, and air in the mediastinum, pericardium, and posterior spinal epidural space.

Treatment:
The patient was treated with broad-spectrum antibiotics, inhalation bronchodilators, systemic corticosteroids, high-flow oxygen, and other supportive measures.

Follow-up care:
The patient is advised to continue monitoring his symptoms, to follow-up with his primary care physician regularly, and to consult with the pulmonologist as needed.

The patient was admitted to the KLE Ayurveda Hospital for treatment of rheumatoid arthritis. She was prescribed Agnitundi vati, Valuka Sweda and Dashanga Lepa as part of her treatment. Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Medical Record Number: [REDACTED]

Final Diagnosis: 
- Streptococcus salivarius meningitis
- Antiphospholipid syndrome
- Cerebrospinal fluid leak (CSF-L)
- Ventriculitis
- Encephalopathy

Hospital Course: 
The patient was admitted to the hospital with acutely worsened headache and new-onset neck and back pain. She had photophobia, chills, and worsening of pain with any flexion of the spine. The laboratory analysis revealed cloudy fluid, a glucose level of less than 10 milligrams per deciliter (mg/dL), protein level of 732 mg/dL, and nucleated cell count of 2764/uL with 87% segmented neutrophils. The CSF Gram stain revealed Gram-positive cocci, and CSF culture grew Streptococcus salivarius. The patient was treated with intravenous (IV) dexamethasone, cefepime, and vancomycin, and lumbar puncture was performed. During her hospitalization, the patient underwent bilateral endoscopic ethmoid repair with lumbar drain placement by otolaryngology and neurosurgery. Her hospital course was complicated by post-repair re-leak and development of ventriculitis. She had a ventriculostomy placed for treatment with a short course of intrathecal antibiotics in addition to a prolonged course of IV antibiotics. Once her CSF studies cleared, she underwent ventriculo-peritoneal shunt placement. Her clinical status improved, and she was ultimately discharged home with minimal neurologic sequelae.

Follow-up Recommendations:
- Follow up with primary care provider for routine monitoring of antiphospholipid syndrome and CSF-L
- Continue taking apixaban as prescribed and monitor for any signs of bleeding
- Follow up with otolaryngologist and neurosurgeon as recommended
- Complete the full course of antibiotics as prescribed
