1. The patient is a 45-year-old female with a history of metastatic germ cell tumor and acute megakaryoblastic leukemia.
2. She presents with pancytopenia, characterized by low leukocyte and platelet counts.
3. A bone marrow trephine biopsy and fine needle aspiration of a cervical lymph node were conducted.
4. She is currently undergoing treatment with daunorubicin and cytarabin.
5. Follow-up appointments are scheduled to monitor her condition.
records.source_note:
Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted for evaluation of easy fatigability and generalized weakness. The medical team suspected a recurrence of metastatic germ cell tumor based on the patient's history. A routine hemogram showed pancytopenia with a total leukocyte count of 3000/μl and a platelet count of 20,000/μl. A bone marrow trephine biopsy showed partial replacement of normal marrow by blasts, megakaryocytes showing multinucleation, and negative staining for myeloperoxidase and leukocyte common antigen. Based on these findings, a diagnosis of acute megakaryoblastic leukemia was made and the patient was treated with daunorubicin and cytarabin.

Six months later, the patient developed a single large cervical lymph node measuring 4×4 cm. A fine needle aspiration (FNA) was done from the cervical swelling which revealed numerous blasts of acute megakaryoblastic leukemia. The patient was treated with three cycles of daunorubicin and cytarabin.

Discharge Summary:

The patient was admitted for evaluation of easy fatigability and generalized weakness with a suspected recurrence of metastatic germ cell tumor. A diagnosis of acute megakaryoblastic leukemia was made based on a bone marrow trephine biopsy and FNA of a cervical lymph node. The patient was treated with daunorubicin and cytarabin and subsequently discharged. Further follow-up appointments will be scheduled to monitor the patient's condition.

records.source_note:
Hospital Course:

The 46-year-old male patient was admitted to the department with complaints of pain and swelling in the maxillary anterior region of the jaw. The patient had previously undergone endodontic treatment for the affected teeth, which initially improved the symptoms. However, the swelling gradually increased in size and was accompanied by dull, throbbing pain from 1 month prior to the visit. 

Diagnostic Findings:

On clinical examination, a solitary diffused extraoral swelling was seen in the upper anterior region of the face, while intraoral examination revealed a solitary well-defined swelling in the maxillary anterior labial vestibule. The swelling was tender on palpation and fluctuant in consistency. The patient also exhibited a slightly deviated tip of the nose along with the elevation of the left nasolabial fold. Radiographic examination revealed the presence of a large, well-defined, corticated periapical radiolucency along with an impacted mesiodens. A dilacerated supernumerary tooth was seen lying horizontally in the radiolucent lesion. 

Treatment:

Based on the patient's medical history, clinical and radiographic evaluations, a provisional diagnosis of an infected dentigerous cyst was made. The lesion was surgically enucleated along with the removal of the impacted mesiodens. Histopathologic examination confirmed the diagnosis of an infected dentigerous cyst.

Summary:

Following surgical intervention, the patient's complaints of pain and swelling in the maxillary anterior region subsided. The patient was discharged from the hospital and advised to maintain good oral hygiene and follow-up visits with their dental care provider.

records.source_note:
Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [Patient Name]
Date of Discharge: [Date]

Hospital Course:
A 62-year-old man who was recently diagnosed with rectal carcinoma was admitted to the hospital for neoadjuvant chemotherapy with 5-FU and leucovorin. On the fourth day of hospitalization, the patient presented to the emergency department with sudden onset of inability to speak, while no other neurological deficits were noted. An MRI was performed during the episode, which showed significant diffusion restriction in the frontal white matter bilaterally and the splenium of the corpus callosum. The 5-FU was ceased, and the patient recovered completely within several hours. The patient remained stable for the rest of their hospital stay and was discharged after being cleared by the medical team.

Summary of Investigations:
MRI was done during admission, revealing significant diffusion restriction in the frontal white matter bilaterally as well as in the splenium of the corpus callosum, in addition to a reduction in the ADC values. However, FLAIR images showed no signal changes. A follow-up MRI done three days after the episode demonstrated significant resolution of findings, with ADC values returning to within normal range.

Final Diagnosis:
In this case, the patient's symptoms and imaging findings were most consistent with a transient ischemic attack (TIA), a brief episode of neurological dysfunction caused by a temporary loss of blood flow to the brain. The 5-FU administered as part of the neoadjuvant chemotherapy may have contributed to the development of TIA.

Treatment Summary:
The 5-FU was ceased as a result of this episode, and the patient was closely monitored for any further developments. No additional treatment was required as the patient fully recovered from the episode and remained stable during the hospital stay.

Follow-up Care:
The patient was discharged after being cleared by the medical team. They were advised to follow-up for a post-discharge visit with their treating oncologist to discuss the future management plan for the rectal carcinoma and the best course of action for chemotherapy. Additionally, the patient was advised to seek emergency medical attention immediately if they experience similar symptoms in the future.

records.source_note:
Discharge Summary

Patient: 70-year-old male with a fractured neck of the femur of the right hip secondary to age-related osteoporosis.

Hospital Course:
The patient presented with hip pain, swelling, and restricted mobility following a fall at home. Clinical and radiological examination revealed a fractured neck of the femur of the right hip secondary to age-related osteoporosis. The patient underwent hemi replacement arthroplasty by posterior approach with a cemented bipolar prosthesis. Postoperatively on the 5th day, the patient experienced clicking in the right hip while walking.

The patient was readmitted to the hospital and further clinical and radiological examinations were performed. Swelling was observed in the hip region with no open wound, scar, or dilated veins. Palpation revealed tenderness over the right Scarpa's area with bitrochanteric compression test positive. No neurological signs or symptoms were observed. Radiographs showed dissociation of the components of the bipolar hemiarthroplasty at the femoral head and neck junction.

Open reduction was performed through the old surgical scar using the posterior approach. The femoral head component was found intraoperatively in the acetabulum and was covered with a well-healed capsule. The tapered part at the inner head and stem neck did not show any scratch marks or defects.

The extracted bipolar prosthesis was removed during surgery.

Outcome:
The patient was followed up for 1 year after revised surgery and is currently asymptomatic with a favorable outcome. A post-operative X-ray of the pelvis shows a new femoral head with longer offset assembled to the old femoral stem.

Abbreviations:
- None.

Patient: 70-year-old male with a fractured neck of the femur of the right hip secondary to age-related osteoporosis.

The patient presented with hip pain, swelling, and restricted mobility following a fall at home. The extracted bipolar prosthesis was removed during surgery.

Outcome:
The patient was followed up for 1 year after revised surgery and is currently asymptomatic with a favorable outcome. A post-operative X-ray of the pelvis shows a new femoral head with longer offset assembled to the old femoral stem.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY

Patient Name: [REDACTED]

Medical Record Number: [REDACTED]

Admission Date: October [REDACTED], 2017

Discharge Date: June [REDACTED], 2019

Hospital Course:

The patient is a 61-year-old male admitted to our hospital in October 2017 for irritable cough without any medical history of interest. A PET-CT was obtained one month later, which showed abnormal increase of glucose metabolism in the lower lobe of the right lung and abnormal high glucose metabolism in the liver, considered as malignant tumor and metastasis respectively. Pathology indicated tumor cells, NapsinA+, thyroid transcription factor-1 (+), alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) (+), Hepa-1 (−), PSA (–), CD10 (−), CD34 showed vessels, CK7 (+), CEA (+), and Ki-67 positive index about 70%. The two tumors were similar in morphology. They confirmed to primary lung adenocarcinoma. The results of gene testing showed EGFR exon 19 deletion mutation. The patient was treated with gefitinib 250mg per os QD in December 2017. The lung focus was observed to have shrunk, considered as partial remission (PR) by clinical evaluation.

However, in April 23, 2018, masses in the lung were larger than before. The gene testing blood was performed again, and the results showed EGFR E19 mutation and MET amplification. The patient was given targeted therapy with gefitinib (250mg per os QD) and crizotinib (250mg per os BID). Lung CT showed the lung focus had shrunk again in June 06, 2018. Moreover, re-examination of chest CT showed recurrent progress of lesions in December 18, 2018. The patient underwent genetic of blood testing again. The results showed that PD-L1 positivity (50%), the tumor mutational burden (high), EGFR E19 mutation and MET amplification. The patient received salvage therapy with immunotherapy (pembrolizumab 100mg intravenous, every 21 days) combined with chemotherapy (pemetrexed 800 mg intravenous + carboplatin 0.4g d2 intravenous, every 28 days, six cycles, then, maintenance of pemetrexed 800 mg alone). CT scan revealed the clinical response with shrinkage of over 30% of the lung lesion on February 27, 2019. Examination of chest CT showed the patient was PR on June 26, 2019. The masses in liver were also significantly smaller than before.

Discharge Diagnosis:

The patient was diagnosed with stage IV non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) with EGFR exon 19 deletion mutation and MET amplification.

Hospital Course Summary:

The patient was admitted to our hospital with irritable cough and was diagnosed with stage IV NSCLC. The patient received targeted therapy with gefitinib, followed by combination therapy with gefitinib and crizotinib. Salvage therapy with immunotherapy and chemotherapy was given, which resulted in significant improvement in the patient's condition. The patient's condition was monitored with regular annual clinical and radiographic follow-ups. At the time of discharge, the patient maintains improved quality of life with no pulmonary symptoms and responded optimally to the treatment.

Discharge Summary:

Admission Date: [date]
Discharge Date: [date]

Admitting Diagnosis: Intractable abdominal pain with diarrhea and vomiting

Principal Diagnosis: Mesenteric ischemia secondary to atypical fibromuscular dysplasia

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted with complaints of intractable abdominal pain, vomiting, and diarrhea. She had a history of hypertension and preeclampsia and had taken oral contraceptive pills (OCPs) for 15 years.

During her hospitalization, she underwent various tests to rule out infectious colitis, vasculitis, hypothyroidism, and inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). A colonoscopy revealed nonspecific findings of diffuse colonic lymphoid reactive hyperplasia, while a small bowel series was negative for inflammation.

Following exposure to OCP medications, mesenteric ischemia was suspected. A magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) of the abdomen revealed proximal superior mesenteric artery (SMA) stenosis, which was confirmed by CT angiogram findings of severe proximal and distal SMA stenosis.

The patient subsequently underwent suboptimal angioplasty, which warranted a 6 × 15 Palmaz Blue Angioplus stent. Her symptoms improved significantly, in that her abdominal pain subsided, and she had an improved tolerance to oral feeds.

She was discharged in stable condition with follow-up instructions.

Discharge Medications:

[Medication list omitted per requirement 5] 

Follow-up Instructions:

1. Follow up with your primary care physician within one week of discharge.
2. Make an appointment with your cardiologist for a follow-up within two weeks of discharge.
3. Dietary instructions: follow a low-fat, low-salt diet.
4. Continue to take any medications prescribed by your physician as directed.
5. Contact your physician immediately if experiencing any concerning symptoms including abdominal pain, shortness of breath, or chest pain.

Hospital Course:

The patient, an 18-year-old male undergraduate student, presented with a disproportionate enlargement of the right lower limb since the age of 10 years, abdominal swelling for the last 5 years, and growth retardation. He was the first issue from a non-consanguineous marriage and had a normal delivery and normal initial growth spurt that slowed down with adolescence. DISCHARGE SUMMARY:

Patient Name: [Name]
DOB: [DOB]

Admission Date: [Admission Date]
Discharge Date: [Discharge Date]

Admitting Diagnosis: Recurrent schwannoma arising from the middle cranial base with sunken eye and drooping of the affected upper eyelid

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 60-year-old woman presented with a recurrent schwannoma arising from the middle cranial base, with sunken eye and drooping of the affected upper eyelid. After observing the results of the first patient's unfavorable findings, the medical team executed a three-stage plan. The first stage included augmenting the eye socket, which was carried out under general anesthesia. In this stage, an autologous ball-shaped graft composed of diced costal cartilage was wrapped with the serratus fascia and transferred to the eye socket. Four months later, the second and third stages were performed under general anesthesia. In the second stage, an auricular cartilage graft was used to correct the lower eyelid retraction, while in the third stage, a fascia lata graft was employed for the frontalis sling to correct the upper eyelid ptosis.
 
The patient had an uneventful postoperative clinical course following the first and second procedures. During the 17-month postoperative follow-up period, the patient has shown an improvement in her aesthetic appearance of the affected eye. However, her enophthalmos has only been partially corrected.

Hospital Outcome:
The patient was discharged without any complications, and further follow-ups were scheduled as per the doctor's advice.

Final Diagnosis:  Recurrent schwannoma arising from the middle cranial base with sunken eye and drooping of the affected upper eyelid

Discharge Medications: N/A

Instructions:
The patient was advised to avoid touching the affected eye and have the follow-ups as scheduled.

Discharge Summary

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
DOB: [REDACTED]
Gender: Male

Clinical History:
The patient is a 22-year-old male with non-seminomatous germinal tumor (NSGT) E-IB. The patient underwent left inguinal orchiectomy, which revealed mixed germ cells including embryonal carcinoma, mature teratoma and seminoma. The patient received two cycles of chemotherapy with bleomycin, etoposide and cisplatin (BEP) and continued yearly follow-up with no evidence of relapse. Eleven years later, the patient underwent neurological consultation due to a sudden loss of visual acuity, which was found to be consistent with multiple sclerosis (MS). The patient received subcutaneous interferon β-1a and showed favorable clinical evolution until routine AFP levels showed an increase and PET scan revealed increased uptake in the left supraclavicular region and both lungs.

Medical Course:
The patient was initially treated with two cycles of BEP therapy, which resulted in disease progression. Subsequently, chemotherapy with BOMP-EPI was administered, yielding a complete response after two cycles. The patient was then considered for intensive chemotherapy and autologous stem cell support but declined and was administered an additional BOMP-EPI cycle as consolidation. After three months, cervical adenopathy was detected by PET and confirmed by fine needle biopsy. Radiotherapy (44 Gy) was subsequently administered, but the patient refused any further treatment. The patient resumed treatment with gemcitabine and initially yielded a good response, but progressive worsening was noted after a follow-up CT scan. Taxol, ifosfamide, and carboplatin therapy were administered with cisplatin substituted for carboplatin. Although there was initial stabilization of pulmonary metastasis after the third cycle, there was subsequent worsening clinical and serological marker progression. Rescue therapy with gemcitabine and oxaliplatin was then administered, but achieved no response, subsequent treatment with etoposide also not yielding a response. After three months, the patient was admitted to hospital with an acute alteration in the level of consciousness that evolved into a coma; a large cerebral hemorrhage was observed and after 48 h, with no neurological improvement despite intensive treatment, the patient succumbed.

Assessment and Plan:
The patient had significant past medical history including NSGT-E1B and MS. The patient had received various chemotherapy, radiation, and drug treatment for MS, and chemotherapy for cancer and had a significantly worsening course. Despite aggressive management, the patient experienced a progressive decline in his overall health over time resulting in his recent passing.

Follow-Up:
The patient passed away while under hospital care. The family has been informed of the patient's passing, and appropriate records have been updated. Further follow-up will be at the discretion of the patient's family.

records.source_note:
Discharge Summary:

Patient: 91-year-old Japanese woman with a history of acute onset type 1 diabetes and absolute insulin deficiency.

Hospital Course:
The patient's recent course was marked by post-meal blood glucose levels of 252 mg/dl and an HbA1c level of 9.6%. The therapeutic regimen included premixed biphasic insulin aspart, miglitol, and aliskiren. Sitagliptin (25 mg/day) was added to better control the diabetes, which resulted in occasional mild hypoglycemia, glucose drinks taken by the patient to manage it, and HbA1c levels reducing from 9.6% to 7.4% over 24 weeks. Due to rising blood pressure, aliskiren was replaced with candesartan.

Outcomes:
The patient's post-meal C-peptide levels remained undetectable (below 0.1 ng/ml) after sitagliptin treatment. No adverse events were observed in kidney or liver function, gastrointestinal complaints, or weight gain.

Follow-up:
No special differences in diet management or physical exercise were noted before and during sitagliptin treatment.

1. Patient is a 40-year-old female admitted with acute abdominal pain, vomiting, and excessive salivation.
2. Admission diagnosis indicates suspected organophosphorus poisoning.
3. Hospital course involved atropine and parenteral hydration, then pralidoxime administration.
4. Clinical findings included constricted pupils, muscle fasciculations, and a prick mark over the right hypochondrium.
5. Diagnostic tests such as blood gas analysis, serum electrolytes, abdominal ultrasound, and CT brain were performed.
6. Diagnostic results were normal in all tests.
7. Treatment was intensive with atropine and pralidoxime, leading to gradual improvement.
8. Patient was discharged after 22 days with full recovery.
9. Discharge status confirmed mobility and complete recovery at 6-week follow-up.
records.source_note:
DISCHARGE SUMMARY

Patient Name: [REDACTED]

Gender: Female                         Date Admitted: [REDACTED]
Age: 40 yrs                                   Date Discharged: [REDACTED]

Admission Diagnosis:
- Suspected organophosphorus poisoning

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted through the emergency department with acute onset of pain abdomen, recurrent vomiting, and excessive salivation followed by altered mental status. Initial investigations were conducted, including atrial blood gas analysis and serum electrolytes which showed normal results. Given a strong suspicion of organophosphorus poisoning, treatment with atropine and parenteral hydration was initiated. The patient eventually confessed to injecting pesticide. Over the next 12 hours, the patient regained consciousness and showed improvements. On day 7, the patient developed delayed onset intermediate syndrome, with worsening of symptoms, and was moved to the intensive care unit. Treatment was intensified with atropine and pralidoxime. Gradual improvement was observed, and the patient was able to discharge from the hospital on day 22.

Clinical Findings:
Physical examination on admission revealed bilateral constricted pupils, muscle fasciculations all over the body, and a pulse of 58 beats per minute. Blood pressure was 100/70 mm Hg, and the abdomen was soft with no localized tenderness, and organomegaly. A prick mark was found over the right hypochondrium during re-examination.

Diagnostic Tests and Results:
- Atrial blood gas analysis and serum electrolytes: normal results
- Ultrasonography of the abdomen and computed tomography (CT) of the brain: normal results
- Plasma cholinesterase level: initially low at 100 units/L, eventually increased to 1530 units/L

Hospital Treatment:
Treatment on admission included atropine 5 mg intravenous (iv) bolus followed by 1 mg hourly infusion, along with parenteral hydration. After the diagnosis of delayed onset intermediate syndrome was made, treatment was intensified with atropine and pralidoxime. The patient's condition gradually improved, and on day 21, the dose of atropine was tapered off, and pralidoxime was stopped. 

Condition on Discharge:
The patient was able to walk without support before discharge from the hospital. On a 6-week follow-up, the patient was able to do her routine work.

Summary:
The patient was admitted with suspected organophosphorus poisoning requiring intensive medical treatment. The patient showed gradual improvement with treatment, leading to discharge from the hospital on day 22. Further follow-up with the patient indicated a full recovery.

records.source_note:
Discharge Summary:

Patient Information:

Name: [Patient’s name]
Age: 38
Gender: Female

Diagnosis:

Recurrent ductal carcinoma in situ of the breast

Hospital Course:

The patient underwent total mastectomy with immediate reconstruction of the breast due to recurrent ductal carcinoma in situ. The patient had previous whole-breast irradiation. The patient elected to receive DIEP flap reconstruction due to being an active runner.

Procedure:

A stacked DIEP flap utilizing both hemi-abdominal flaps was performed for the patient. Two single perforators were chosen on each hemi-abdomen and were dissected down to their respective deep inferior epigastric pedicles. One set of deep inferior epigastric vessels was anastomosed to the antegrade internal mammary vessels, whereas the other set of vessels was anastomosed to the retrograde internal mammary vessels. The folded flap was then inset in a stacked manner to maximize volume and projection.

Outcomes:

The patient had a satisfactory aesthetic outcome with a good size match achieved without any fat necrosis. Computed tomographic angiogram of the chest was performed incidentally for respiratory concerns on postoperative day 5 and revealed patent vascular anastomoses to both pedicles.

Follow-up:

The patient was discharged from the hospital with appropriate wound care and follow-up appointments with her surgeon. A one-year follow-up was performed and the patient reported a satisfactory aesthetic outcome with no complications.

Computed tomographic angiogram of the chest showed patent vascular anastomoses to both pedicles. There were no reported postoperative complications in the discharge summary.

Discharge Summary

Patient Name: N/A
Medical Record Number: N/A
Sex: Female
Age: 35 years

Hospital Course: 
The patient was admitted to our department with a breast nodule in the upper right region. She had a history of stage IV B mediastinal large B-cell lymphoma, which was treated with high-dose sequential (HDS) chemotherapy and autologous stem-cell transplantation a year ago with complete remission. Initial investigations including computed tomography scans and positron emission tomography showed a positive uptake of radiotracer in the right breast suggesting a recurrent disease. A mammography revealed a solitary ill-defined mass in the upper outer quadrant of the right breast. The lesion was surgically removed, and it was diagnosed as myeloid sarcoma based on morphologic and phenotypic findings.

Subsequent laboratory investigations showed normal blood counts with no blasts in the peripheral blood, no evidence of leukemic infiltration in bone marrow aspirates, and a normal karyotype. The patient underwent radiotherapy and two courses of high-dose cytarabine. However, the disease had a relapse after 5 months and pursued a fulminant course with the patient's death.

- Admitted with a breast nodule in the upper right region.
- History of stage IV B mediastinal large B-cell lymphoma treated with high-dose sequential (HDS) chemotherapy and autologous stem-cell transplantation with complete remission.
- Diagnosis of myeloid sarcoma based on morphologic and phenotypic findings.
- Normal blood counts with no blasts in the peripheral blood, no evidence of leukemic infiltration in bone marrow aspirates, and a normal karyotype.
- Treatment with radiotherapy and two courses of high-dose cytarabine.
- Disease relapsed after 5 months and pursued a fulminant course with the patient's death.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [Name]
Medical Record Number: [Number]
Admission Date: [Date]
Discharge Date: [Date]

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to the national hospital of Sri Lanka on September [Date] with symptoms of dizziness, nausea, vomiting, and headache. On examination, the patient was drowsy, but oriented and rational with orange-red discoloration of the face, hands, and feet. No evidence of asterixis or coagulopathy was found. The patient had a history of deliberate self-harm after a domestic dispute by ingesting 28 tablets of FDC-IR, containing 4.2 g of standard INH and 7.2 g of rifampicin, prescribed for her uncle. The family had attempted induced emesis at home, unsuccessfully. The patient developed generalized tonic-clonic seizure, lasting about 3 minutes while being seen in the medical ward, and was given IV diazepam 5 mg immediately. She was then transferred to the national hospital of Sri Lanka immediately for further care.

The arterial blood gas analysis was pH 7.36, HCO3- 20 mmol/L, PCO2 24 mmHg, pO2 135 mmHg, Base excess -5, lactate level 2.3 and O2 saturation100%.

The patient was initially treated with crushed oral tablets of pyridoxine 4.2 g (equal to INAH dose ingested) administered via a nasogastric tube and forced diuresis was commenced using IV 0.9% saline in order to enhance excretion of toxic metabolites via kidneys. The patient received supportive care for acute liver injury that occurred on Day 2. Her liver functions started to deteriorate from Day 2 with persistent anorexia and vomiting and gradually started to improve by Day 7 of admission. The patient made a complete recovery and was discharged on Day 10 of the hospital admission. The patient's liver functions were found to be normal 1 week after discharge.

Hospital Course Summary:

Admission Date: [DATE] Discharge Date: [DATE]

Patient Name: [NAME]                  Medical Record Number: [MR NUMBER]

Admitting Diagnosis: Acute reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome (RCVS)

Brief Summary of Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted to the hospital due to sudden onset of thunderclap headache for the last three days. Computed tomography angiography (CTA) showed segmental stenosis of the left vertebra artery (VA). After two days, magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) showed newly developed multiple arterial stenosis on both anterior cerebral arteries (ACA) of left A1 segment, right proximal A2 segment, and both middle cerebral arteries (MCA). After further tests and examinations, it was diagnosed that the patient had acute reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome (RCVS) and her levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system (IUS) was suspected to be associated with RCVS. Nimodipine was prescribed and the levonorgestrel-releasing IUS was removed from her. The patient's headache gradually improved, and the follow-up tests showed a positive recovery. The stenosis disappeared in one year follow-up MRA.

Hospital Course:

Admission:

The patient presented with a thunderclap headache for the last three days. The patient had not been diagnosed with migraine before and had severe headaches once or twice a month since the levonorgestrel-releasing IUS was inserted in November 2016. The patient took NSAIDS or acetaminophen when there was a headache.

Investigations:

Computed tomography angiography (CTA) revealed segmental stenosis of the left vertebra artery (VA). In TCD, increased mean flow velocities (MFV) were recorded from both middle cerebral arteries. Magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) showed newly developed multiple arterial stenosis on both anterior cerebral arteries (ACA) of left A1 segment, right proximal A2 segment, and both middle cerebral arteries (MCA). In an additional TCD examination, the MFV of the right MCA and left ACA was increased in accordance with the MRA results. One week later, follow-up CTA showed stenosis on the right ACA and a newly developed stenosis on the right VA, stenosis on both MCAs were resolved. At follow-up TCD after one month, the MFV of both MCA and left ACA was normalized in accordance with the CTA results.

Diagnosis and Treatment:

The patient was diagnosed with acute reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome (RCVS) and considered that RCVS is associated with the levonorgestrel-releasing IUS. The patient was prescribed nimodipine, and the levonorgestrel-releasing IUS was removed from her. The patient's headache gradually improved, and the follow-up tests showed a positive recovery. The stenosis disappeared in one year follow-up MRA.

Discharge Condition:

The patient was discharged in improved condition with resolved symptoms.

Follow-up:

The patient is advised to follow-up with the healthcare provider after the prescribed course of treatment for any further instructions.

records.source_note:
Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: N/A
Date of Admission: 12/2016
Date of Discharge: N/A
Length of Stay: N/A
Medical Record Number: N/A

Hospital Course: 
The patient was referred to our institution in December 2016 for pulmonary metastatic relapse after receiving multiple lines of chemotherapy and radiation therapy elsewhere. A high-throughput molecular screening trial was conducted, and a pulmonary biopsy was performed to confirm the diagnosis of metastasis from the primary tumor of the patient: malignant tumors in the pulmonary artery evoking a myxoma - Pleomorphic angiosarcoma (PAIS). It was found that the tumor contained MDM2 amplification associated with CDK4 amplification. The patient was started on a 4th-line chemotherapy based on the combination of carboplatin and vinorelbine in February 2017. After nine cycles, the patient's performance status (PS) was zero without any clinical symptom. However, a CT scan showed disease progression with an increase in size of two lesions.

Hospital Course Summary:
The patient was diagnosed with Pleomorphic Angiosarcoma of the pulmonary artery consistent morphologically with PAIS. The patient received multiple lines of chemotherapy and radiation therapy elsewhere before being referred to our institution. After conducting a high-throughput molecular screening trial, the patient was started on a 4th-line chemotherapy based on carboplatin and vinorelbine. Although the treatment was well tolerated and the patient's PS returned to zero, a CT scan revealed disease progression. The next step in the treatment plan will be the administration of stereotactic radiotherapy on both progressive lesions.

records.source_note:
Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: N/A
Age: 9 months
Sex: Male

Clinical Course:
The patient presented with an 8-day history of watery, non-bloody diarrhea, vomiting, and decreased oral intake. Initial investigations showed leukocytosis, anemia, thrombocytopenia, and evidence of microangiopathic hemolysis. Abdominal ultrasound revealed echogenic but normal-sized kidneys confirming the diagnosis of hemolytic uremic syndrome. Peritoneal dialysis was initiated after a lack of response to high doses of intravenous furosemide. The results of stool studies were positive for Norovirus GI/G II. Massive albuminuria and low complement levels were also observed.

Treatment Provided:
The patient underwent continuous peritoneal dialysis for five days, and one unit of packed red blood cells was transfused. No medication or treatment plan information was provided in the case report.

Outcome:
The patient improved steadily, and both kidney function and albuminuria normalized by the 10th day following the onset of the disease. C3 and C4 complement levels returned to normal levels three weeks after the onset of the disease. The patient was followed for 11 months with no signs of residual damage, normotensive, and no microalbuminuria.

Diagnosis:
The patient was diagnosed with hemolytic uremic syndrome likely caused by Norovirus GI/G II.

Follow-Up:
The patient's parents were advised to continue with regular pediatrician visits and a healthy diet and lifestyle. Follow-up testing and monitoring were not mentioned in the case report.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [insert patient name]
Gender: Male
Age: 41 years old
Date of Admission: [insert date]
Date of Discharge: [insert date]

Reason for Admission:
The patient was admitted to the Center of Trauma Surgery for the closure of an open infected wound on his right lower limb caused by an accidental explosion.

Hospital Course:
Upon admission, the patient's blood pressure was 99/50 mmHg, pulse rate was 102 beats per minutes, and respiratory rate was 21 breaths per minute. His medical history revealed no chronic medical conditions and he denied any unhealthy behaviors.

The patient underwent aggressive fluid administration, hemodynamic support, and intravenously administered antibiotic therapy. Two surgical procedures were performed, including debridement of the wounds and excision of necrotic muscles. The wounds were then closed with VSD and adhesive membrane and connected to negative pressure drainage equipment. Stretching treatment was applied to the healthy skin around the wound to facilitate approximation to the wound margins. The VSD was reapplied to close the wound as before.

Upon monitoring the wound, the size decreased from 40 cm × 35 cm to 1.0 cm × 0.8 cm within the span of eighteen days after the last operation. The patient was ambulatory and showed no evidence of damage to the skin margins.

Based on the patient's progress and healing, he was discharged from the hospital with instructions for continued outpatient care.

Discharge Condition:
Upon discharge, the patient's wounds had significantly decreased in size and had healed according to medical standards. The patient had regained his ability to ambulate freely and perform certain activities.

Instructions for Outpatient Care:
The patient is advised to maintain the wound site clean and covered with dressings, if necessary. The patient should avoid overexertion and seek medical attention if any complications or concerns arise.

Follow-Up:
The patient is recommended to follow up with his primary care physician for ongoing wound care and management. Additionally, the patient should continue to monitor his health and exercise preventative measures as recommended by medical professionals.

Initial Clinical Summary:

[Patient Name] is a 41-year-old male admitted to the Center of Trauma Surgery for the management of an open, infected wound on his right lower limb, resulting from an accidental explosion. His vital signs upon admission were BP 99/50 mmHg, pulse 102 bpm, and respiratory rate 21 bpm. The patient's medical history is unremarkable, and he denies any unhealthy behaviors.

Upon admission, the patient underwent aggressive fluid administration, hemodynamic support, and intravenous antibiotic therapy. Two surgical procedures were performed: debridement of the wounds and excision of necrotic muscles. Wounds were subsequently closed with VSD and adhesive membrane and connected to negative pressure drainage equipment. Stretching treatment was applied to the healthy skin around the wound to facilitate approximation to the wound margins.

The wound size decreased from 40 cm × 35 cm to 1.0 cm × 0.8 cm within eighteen days of surgery. The patient was ambulatory and showed no evidence of damage to the skin margins. Upon discharge, the patient's wounds had significantly decreased in size and had healed according to medical standards.

The patient is advised to maintain the wound site clean and covered with dressings, if necessary. He should avoid overexertion and seek medical attention if any complications or concerns arise. The patient is recommended to follow up with his primary care physician for ongoing wound care and management.

records.source_note:
Hospital Course:

The 85-year-old Japanese woman with squamous cell lung carcinoma was admitted with rapidly worsening general fatigue and appetite loss eight days after receiving the eighth cycle of pembrolizumab monotherapy. She had been diagnosed with Stage IV squamous cell lung cancer seven months prior. Pembrolizumab had been administered as the first-line therapy, resulting in stable disease. Routine examination before each infusion had shown no significant changes up to the eighth cycle.

Physical Examination:

On physical examination, the patient was debilitated, but there were no remarkable findings for the head, neck, chest, abdomen, or extremities. No visual deficit was apparent according to the confrontation method.

Laboratory Examination:

Laboratory examination on arrival revealed a low serum cortisol level with an inappropriately low ACTH level, hyponatremia with a raised antidiuretic hormone (ADH) level, and hypoglycemia, but no eosinophilia. Urine osmolarity was inappropriately high despite low plasma osmolarity, indicating inappropriate ADH secretion. There was a poor response to standard-dose short ACTH testing. Serum anti-pituitary cell antibody-1 was negative. Urinary free cortisol excretion was low.

Diagnosis and Treatment:

The patient was diagnosed with isolated ACTH deficiency. Hydrocortisone administered swiftly improved the patient's general condition, corrected the inappropriately high ADH level, and normalized serum sodium concentration. The adrenal glands were unremarkable on computed tomography. The patient was discharged and followed monthly in outpatient care.

Follow-Up:

Cortisol levels ranged from 8.12 to 18.3 μg/dL, while ACTH levels were not detectable on any occasion during the observation period 5 months after admission. Thus, ACTH deficiency obviously persisted while thyroid function remained normal, and white blood cell count, eosinophil count, serum electrolytes, and glucose were all unremarkable.

The patient showed persistent ACTH deficiency and was followed up monthly in outpatient care with unremarkable electrolytes and glucose levels.

5. Ophthalmological evaluation revealed worsening refractive error.
6. Diagnosis confirmed topiramate-induced acute myopia.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
DOB: [REDACTED]
Date of Admission: [REDACTED]
Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]

Hospital Course Summary:

Admission:
The patient, a 35-year-old female, was admitted to the hospital with a complaint of worsening headaches. The initial diagnosis was migraine, for which she had been previously treated with propranolol and flunarazine. The patient was advised to continue the flunarazine and discharged.

Readmission:
The patient was readmitted one month later with persistent headaches. She complained of acute onset blurring of vision. An ophthalmological examination revealed a bilateral refractive error of -0.5 diopters. Topiramate was then prescribed, which the patient took for two weeks. The patient's visual symptoms persisted and it was suspected that the topiramate was the source of her acute symptoms. The drug was discontinued and the patient was referred back to the ophthalmologist, where her refractive error had worsened to approximately -3.5 diopters bilaterally.

Discharge:
The patient was diagnosed with topiramate-induced acute myopia. An ophthalmologist review two weeks later found no concerns. 

Follow-up:
The patient was advised not to take topiramate again. Follow-up was arranged with her general practitioner and ophthalmologist. 

Diagnostic Test Results:
- Neurological examination: normal
- Ophthalmological examination: bilateral refractive error of -0.5 diopters
- Vision: 6/6
- Intraocular pressure: normal

Diagnosis:
- Topiramate induced acute myopia

Treatment:
- Discontinuation of topiramate

Discharge Medications:
- Not applicable

Discharge Condition:
The patient's condition had significantly improved and she was discharged with no complaints. 

Discharge Instructions:
The patient was advised to attend follow-up appointments with her general practitioner and ophthalmologist. She was also instructed not to take topiramate again.

records.source_note:
Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [redacted]
Medical Record Number: [redacted]
Date of Admission: [redacted]
Date of Discharge: [redacted]

Admission Diagnosis: Epigastric pain, vomiting
Discharge Diagnosis: Symptomatic cystic lymphangioma originating from the left adrenal gland

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted with complaints of constant epigastric pain that was not related to food intake. The pain was accompanied by multiple episodes of vomiting. Ultrasonography and a CT scan were performed, which showed a cystic-like retroperitoneal mass on the left side. The patient underwent a CT-guided puncture of the cyst, but it could not be completely evacuated due to technical problems. Cytology came back negative for malignant cells and was compatible with a cystic lymphangioma.

To assess the location of the retroperitoneal cyst more precisely, the patient underwent a magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). T2-weighted turbo spin-echo MR-sequences showed a lesion compatible with a cystic lymphangioma originating from the left adrenal gland. Due to persisting invalidating pain, a surgical resection of this cystic lesion was proposed. During surgery, the adrenal origin of the cyst was confirmed, and an “en bloc” left adrenalectomy was performed without rupture of the cyst. The postoperative course was uneventful, and the patient was discharged on postoperative day 5.

Follow-up:
The patient was seen at the outpatient clinic one month after the surgery and described no more symptoms. The final diagnosis of cystic lymphangioma originating from the left adrenal gland was confirmed by histopathology combined with immunohistochemistry.

Differential Diagnosis:
Primary adrenal tumors, metastatic adenocarcinomas, angiosarcomas, multicystic mesotheliomas, or adrenal cysts were considered in the differential diagnosis.

Treatment:
Surgical resection represents the definitive treatment if the cystic lymphangioma is symptomatic. Complete resection of the cyst is recommended, and associated parenchymal resection (adrenalectomy) depends on the location of the cyst and on the intraoperative dissection.

Discharge Condition:
The patient was discharged in stable condition and instructed to follow up as an outpatient.

Follow-up Plan:
The patient was advised to return to the outpatient clinic for follow-up consultations.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [redacted]
Medical Record Number: [redacted]
Date of Admission: [redacted]
Date of Discharge: [redacted]

Admission Diagnosis: Epigastric pain, vomiting
Discharge Diagnosis: Symptomatic cystic lymphangioma originating from the left adrenal gland

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted with complaints of constant epigastric pain that was not related to food intake. The pain was accompanied by multiple episodes of vomiting. Ultrasonography and a CT scan were performed, which showed a cystic-like retroperitoneal mass on the left side. The patient underwent a CT-guided puncture of the cyst, but it could not be completely evacuated due to technical problems. Cytology came back negative for malignant cells and was compatible with a cystic lymphangioma.

To assess the location of the retroperitoneal cyst more precisely, the patient underwent a magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). T2-weighted turbo spin-echo MR-sequences showed a lesion compatible with a cystic lymphangioma originating from the left adrenal gland. Due to persisting invalidating pain, a surgical resection of this cystic lesion was proposed. During surgery, the adrenal origin of the cyst was confirmed, and an “en bloc” left adrenalectomy was performed without rupture of the cyst. The postoperative course was uneventful, and the patient was discharged on postoperative day 5.

Follow-up:
The patient was seen at the outpatient clinic one month after the surgery and described no more symptoms. The final diagnosis of cystic lymphangioma originating from the left adrenal gland was confirmed by histopathology combined with immunohistochemistry.

Differential Diagnosis:
Primary adrenal tumors, metastatic adenocarcinomas, angiosarcomas, multicystic mesotheliomas, or adrenal cysts were considered in the differential diagnosis.

Treatment:
Surgical resection represents the definitive treatment if the cystic lymphangioma is symptomatic. Complete resection of the cyst is recommended, and associated parenchymal resection (adrenalectomy) depends on the location of the cyst and on the intraoperative dissection.

Discharge Condition:
The patient was discharged in stable condition and instructed to follow up as an outpatient.

Follow-up Plan:
The patient was advised to return to the outpatient clinic for follow-up consultations.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [Redacted]
Date of Admission: [Redacted]
Date of Discharge: [Redacted]
Length of Stay: [Redacted]

Diagnosis:
The patient was diagnosed with Gross Hydronephrosis (GH) caused by obstruction from a kidney stone at the junction of the ureter and renal pelvis, accompanied by renal cell transitional cell carcinoma (T2N0M0).

Hospital Course:
The patient presented with a gradual increase in abdominal girth over the past two years, along with abdominal distension and intermittent nausea for the past six months. The patient also experienced repeated intractable hiccups for two months, leading to the hospital admission. Physical examination revealed a longitudinal surgical scar on the upper abdomen and a swelling of the mass on the left side of the abdomen.

Further diagnostic investigations were performed, including ultrasonography, computerized tomography (CT), and an isotope kidney scan. These tests revealed the presence of a massive hypoechoic lesion occupying almost the entire abdomen, exerting pressure on the stomach, liver, pancreas, and spleen. Adhesion between the kidney and surrounding organs was evident during the laparoscopy and open simple nephrectomy procedure.

About 7.5 liters of hydronephrosis fluid were drained, and the left kidney and upper ureter were successfully removed, resulting in the disappearance of long-lasting hiccups and improvement of the patient's appetite and overall health. After the operation, the patient was observed for six months, during which there was no recurrence of the hiccups.

Discharge Instructions:
The patient was discharged with instructions to follow a proper diet and continue with regular follow-up appointments with the healthcare professional.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Age: 18 months
Sex: Female

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted with a history of mild fever and intermittent discharge from a sinus in the mid-dorsal area. She underwent a dorsal D1 to D8 laminectomy, mid-line myelotomy, and total tumor excision under microscope. During the intra-operative period, a bolus dose of injection methylprednisolone was administered, followed by 24-hour post-operative administration with a dose of 5.4 mg/kg body weight.

Clinical Findings:

On examination, the patient was febrile with normal power and sensation in all limbs except mild stiffness of the left leg. A skin dimple with no active discharge was observed at presentation in the posterior aspect of the mid-dorsal spine (D5) []. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the whole spine revealed a large intramedullary cystic lesion in the dorsal segment of the spinal cord extending from D2 to D7 vertebral level with a single posterior sinus tract opening to skin at D5 vertebral level. The cystic lesion showed T1-weighted (T1W) hypointense, T2-weighted (T2W) and short tau inversion recovery (STIR) hyperintense signal, restricted diffusion in diffusion-weighted image (DWI) and apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) image. Small T1W isointense and T2W hypointense content noted inside the cystic lesion. No fat signal was seen inside the mass. Post-contrast MRI imaging showed no enhancement of the lesion [].

Treatment and Progress:

A tuft of hair and cheesy material with a thin capsule were removed in piecemeal, and a portion of the capsule could not be removed as it was densely adhered to the cord. The dermal sinus tract was ending within the dermoid capsule, and it was also excised. Myelotomy was left open, and water-tight dural closure was done. Post-operatively, the patient developed mild weakness of the left lower limb (grade-IV power), which she recovered by the 10th post-operative day. The histopathological diagnosis of the lesion confirmed dermoid cyst [].

Summary:

The patient was admitted with mild fever and intermittent discharge from a sinus in the mid-dorsal area. She underwent a dorsal D1 to D8 laminectomy, mid-line myelotomy, and total tumor excision under microscope with intra-operative and post-operative administration of injection methylprednisolone. Post-operatively, she developed mild weakness of the left lower limb, which she recovered by the 10th post-operative day. The histopathological diagnosis of the lesion confirmed dermoid cyst.

2. The tumor showed low Ki-67 expression (<3%) and was characterized by chromogranin and synaptophysin positivity.
3. The patient underwent multiple treatments including chemotherapy, surgery, and endocrine therapy.
4. He developed mesenteric lymph nodes with lymphocytic involvement and abdominal nodal disease on PET scan.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY
Patient Name: [Redacted]
Medical Record Number: [Redacted]
Admission Date: September 2004
Discharge Date: N/A

HOSPITAL COURSE:

The patient is a 41-year-old male who presented in September 2004 with an episode of acute gastrointestinal bleeding that was associated with non-Hodgkin's lymphoma with a nonspecific subtype. He was transferred to a larger center to receive chemotherapy to avoid a surgical procedure. He was treated with three cycles of R-CHOP, without clinical response. He was then submitted to a surgical procedure, and the anatomopathological study of retroperitoneal lymph nodes was consistent with an infiltrative carcinoma. The immunohistochemical analysis revealed chromogranin and synaptophysin expression and also a Ki 67 < 3%. A low-grade neuroendocrine tumor was confirmed after the review was performed in both specimens due to the discordance between the two biopsies regarding the histological diagnoses. The patient was then treated with octreotide acetate until clinical recovery and then, without any clinical or radiological evidence of disease, treatment was withheld. 

On December 2010, he presented with an abdominal obstructive syndrome, and an exploratory laparotomy was necessary. The anatomopathological diagnosis of mesenteric lymph nodes resected was consistent with areas containing marginal zone B-cell lymphoma/chronic lymphocytic leukemia and neuroendocrine tumor. Bone marrow was not infiltrated, and FDG-PET showed exclusively abdominal nodal disease which was compatible with lymphoma involvement. At this time he was treated with 6 cycles of CHOP, and octreotide was started again. CT scan obtained at the end of the treatment showed complete response.

FAMILY HISTORY:

The patient's family history revealed his father's prostate cancer and that the majority of his father's brothers presented lymphoma or leukemia.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION:

At clinical examination, the patient lacked any cutaneous stigma of neurofibromatosis, but one of the CT scans revealed the presence of various neurofibromas in the thorax and abdomen.

DIAGNOSIS:

The patient was diagnosed with low-grade neuroendocrine tumor, CLL, and marginal zone B-cell lymphoma/chronic lymphocytic leukemia.

TREATMENT:

The patient was treated with octreotide acetate until clinical recovery, 3 cycles of R-CHOP, 6 cycles of CHOP, and octreotide was started again. CLL is under clinical surveillance, and the patient is out of treatment in the moment. 

DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS:

The patient should continue following up with his healthcare provider to monitor his CLL and for any future medical concerns.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY
Patient Name: [Redacted]
Medical Record Number: [Redacted]
Admission Date: September 2004
Discharge Date: N/A

HOSPITAL COURSE:

The patient is a 41-year-old male who presented in September 2004 with an episode of acute gastrointestinal bleeding that was associated with non-Hodgkin's lymphoma with a nonspecific subtype. He was transferred to a larger center to receive chemotherapy to avoid a surgical procedure. He was treated with three cycles of R-CHOP, without clinical response. He was then submitted to a surgical procedure, and the anatomopathological study of retroperitoneal lymph nodes was consistent with an infiltrative carcinoma. The immunohistochemical analysis revealed chromogranin and synaptophysin expression and also a Ki 67 < 3%. A low-grade neuroendocrine tumor was confirmed after the review was performed in both specimens due to the discordance between the two biopsies regarding the histological diagnoses. The patient was then treated with octreotide acetate until clinical recovery and then, without any clinical or radiological evidence of disease, treatment was withheld. 

On December 2010, he presented with an abdominal obstructive syndrome, and an exploratory laparotomy was necessary. The anatomopathological diagnosis of mesenteric lymph nodes resected was consistent with areas containing marginal zone B-cell lymphoma/chronic lymphocytic leukemia and neuroendocrine tumor. Bone marrow was not infiltrated, and FDG-PET showed exclusively abdominal nodal disease which was compatible with lymphoma involvement. At this time he was treated with 6 cycles of CHOP, and octreotide was started again. CT scan obtained at the end of the treatment showed complete response.

FAMILY HISTORY:

The patient's family history revealed his father's prostate cancer and that the majority of his father's brothers presented lymphoma or leukemia.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION:

At clinical examination, the patient lacked any cutaneous stigma of neurofibromatosis, but one of the CT scans revealed the presence of various neurofibromas in the thorax and abdomen.

DIAGNOSIS:

The patient was diagnosed with low-grade neuroendocrine tumor, CLL, and marginal zone B-cell lymphoma/chronic lymphocytic leukemia.

TREATMENT:

The patient was treated with octreotide acetate until clinical recovery, 3 cycles of R-CHOP, 6 cycles of CHOP, and octreotide was started again. CLL is under clinical surveillance, and the patient is out of treatment in the moment. 

DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS:

The patient should continue following up with his healthcare provider to monitor his CLL and for any future medical concerns.

Discharge Summary

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Medical Record Number: [REDACTED]
Date of Admission: [REDACTED]
Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]

Hospital Course:

The patient, a 10-year-old female with known 22q11DS, was admitted to our otorhinolaryngologic department for 8 years. Relevant medical history includes cardiac anomalies, conductive hearing loss bilaterally, malformed ossicular chain, and narrow ear canals. Tympanostomy tube placement was done at the age of 3 years, and the patient wore hearing aids since the age of 4.

The patient underwent a middle ear inspection and ossicular reconstruction on the left side due to conductive hearing loss and difficulty in wearing hearing aids with glasses. CT scan was pre-operatively performed, which showed epitympanic ossicular fixation and a more horizontal orientation of the incus and dehiscent facial nerve canal on the left side.

A retroauricular incision was made, and the external auditory canal was saucerized and widened both anteriorly and posteriorly. Therapeutic intervention included curetting the epitympanic fixation of the malleus, removing the manubrium of the malleus, which was atrophic and anteriorly fixated, to result in a mobile ossicular chain. Audiometry tests showed a hearing improvement of frequencies 0.25, 5, 1, and 2 kHz.

The patient was discharged with no complications, and follow-up was advised.

Diagnoses:

1. Known 22q11DS
2. Cardiac anomalies
3. Conductive hearing loss bilaterally
4. Malformed ossicular chain
5. Narrow ear canals
6. Epitympanic ossicular fixation on the left side
7. More horizontal orientation of the incus on the left side

records.source_note:
Hospital Course:

The patient, a 65-year-old male with diabetes, hypertension, and spinal cord injury, presented with high fever on postoperative day 10 after undergoing partial lung resection for adenocarcinoma. CT scan revealed empyema, and Streptococcus caprae was detected by wound culture. The patient underwent irrigation and thoracic drainage, as well as broad-spectrum antibiotic treatment for 16 days. Although the cavity was reducing in size, the infection persisted.

Consultation:

Plastic surgeons were consulted, and on postoperative day 36, non-open wound therapy with Negative Pressure Wound Therapy with instillation (NPWTi-d) was installed. The patient received this treatment continuously for 20 days until the CT scan confirmed that the empyema disappeared.

Follow Up:

Four months after completing non-OWT NPWTi-d, his CT scan showed no empyema recurrence. The patient was discharged with instructions to follow up with his primary care physician for regular check-ups. 

The patient received high-quality care throughout the hospital stay, and the multidisciplinary team made appropriate referrals and consultations, leading to successful treatment of empyema with no further recurrence.

Referral to plastic surgeons for consultation also played a key role in successful treatment. Regular check-ups with the primary care physician were advised for follow-up and recurrence prevention.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Information:
Name: Five-year-old female cousin of Case-2
Medical Record Number: Not provided

Hospital Course:
The patient presented with minimal skin lesions and abnormal gait, but normal intelligence. An additional radiographic study was conducted, which included AP and lateral skull, AP spine, AP shoulder joint, and AP hands. The two children with severe ISH showed abnormal craniofacial contour. Case-1 showed brachycephaly and partial closure of coronals/lambdoid. Case-2 showed scaphocephaly with sagittal suture synostosis. The 3D reconstruction CT of the skull of Case-2 showed total synostosis of the sagittal suture with mild plagiocephaly. AP spine and shoulder radiograph of Case-1 showed severe osteolysis of the shoulder and hip joints were noted. AP spine radiograph of Case-4 displayed a less important malformation complex except for bilateral and symmetrical hypoplasia of the clavicles. The skeletal phenotype of Case-1 with severe type of ISH, AP radiographs of the shoulders, humero-radial, and pelvis showed multiple dislocations secondary to massive osteolysis along the major joints of the shoulders, elbows, and hips. AP pelvis radiograph of Case-5 showed "shepherd's crook" deformity with severe form of coxa vara.

Conclusion:
The patient presented with a unique skeletal phenotype characterized by abnormal craniofacial contour, severe osteolysis in shoulder and hip joints, and deformed pelvis. The patient underwent a comprehensive radiographic study that showed brachycephaly, scaphocephaly, total synostosis of the sagittal suture, and severe osteolysis. Further diagnostic and therapeutic interventions may be required.

Discharge Summary:
Patient Name: Anonymous

Date of Admission: June 25, 2009

Date of Discharge: Ongoing

Hospital: Not disclosed 

Admission Diagnosis:
Squamous cell carcinoma

Hospital Course Summary:

The 81-year-old Japanese male patient was admitted to our hospital with a chief complaint of pain in the right lingual margin caused by a mass. The contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) revealed an enhanced soft tissue mass at the right lingual margin. On biopsy of the lingual mass, the patient was diagnosed with squamous cell carcinoma and underwent tumor resection of the right lingual site under general anesthesia.

After eight months, follow-up contrast-enhanced CT scan detected a swelling in the right upper cervical region. Therefore, the patient underwent RND under general anesthesia according to the traditional method. Adjuvant chemotherapy was planned but stopped due to patient's poor physical condition.

Six months after right RND, a pathologic fracture with bone destruction in the proximal end of the right clavicle was detected in contrast-enhanced CT scan. The patient suspected bone metastasis from the tongue cancer as a possible cause. However, after conducting 18F-fluorodeoxyglcose (FDG) positron emission tomography (PET)-CT, it was concluded that the probability of metastasis was very low. Ultrasonography (US) on October 5, 2010, showed that the clavicle fracture (CF) was likely to have been caused by non-neoplastic changes.

Four follow-up contrast-enhanced CT scans were carried out over the following 6 years, with no signs of recurrence or metastasis of the malignant tumor. The CF was monitored for separation between the bone fragments and managed with a watch and wait approach.

Discharge Condition:
The patient's condition is stable, and no signs of recurrence or metastasis have been detected over the following 6 years. 

Recommendations:
The patient should continue to undergo regular follow-up contrast-enhanced CT scans to monitor the CF and ensure that there are no signs of cancer recurrence or metastasis.

The patient was admitted to the hospital with a history of hypertension, high cholesterol, coronary artery disease with surgical intervention six months ago, and two episodes of cough with hemoptysis associated with some chest discomfort. The patient was evaluated with laboratory tests and electrocardiogram, and a computed tomography scan of the chest with contrast was performed to rule out pulmonary embolism. The scan showed the presence of a pseudoaneurysm in the SVG graft to RCA, which was located 2 cm from its origin, measuring 1.2 cm in size with adjacent fluid. A decision was made to repair the pseudoaneurysm through percutaneous approach with polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE)-covered Jostent GraftMaster after a multi-disciplinary meeting. The patient underwent successful intracoronary stenting of the graft with no procedural complications.

Discharge Diagnosis:
The patient has a history of hypertension, high cholesterol, and coronary artery disease with surgical intervention six months ago. The diagnosis at discharge is pseudoaneurysm of the SVG graft.

Discharge Instructions:
The patient is advised to continue dual antiplatelet therapy as prescribed by the healthcare provider. The patient is advised to follow up with the healthcare provider as scheduled.

Follow-up Plan:
The patient is scheduled for follow-up angiogram in six months.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Medical Record Number: [REDACTED]
Date of Admission: [REDACTED]
Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]

History of Present Illness: 
The patient is a 53-year-old male who presented with upper abdominal discomfort and meteorism accompanied by seldom vomiting. The symptoms arose roughly two hours after meals and lasted for hours. The initial diagnosis was biliary colic and dyspepsia.

Hospital Course:
Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a pseudo kidney image in the transverse colon, and abdominal tomography showed a 9 cm segment of diffuse thickening of the transverse colon wall along with colocolic intussusception. Endoscopic examination showed an intraluminal fatty lesion leading to intussusception in the distal segments of the transverse colon accompanied by nonnecrotizing intussusception. To be treated, the patient underwent left hemicolectomy with end-to-end anastomosis. The postoperative course was uneventful, and the patient was discharged on his sixth postoperative day.

Diagnostic Assessment:
Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a pseudo kidney image in the transverse colon. Abdominal tomography showed diffuse thickening of the transverse colon wall along a 9 cm segment and colocolic intussusception. Endoscopic examination revealed an intraluminal fatty lesion leading to intussusception in the distal segments of the transverse colon accompanied by nonnecrotizing intussusception. Histopathologic examination of the specimen revealed a lipomatous lesion with a diameter of 5 cm. The lipomatous lesion was of pure benign nature. There were 11 lymph nodes without any signs of malignancy.

Condition at Discharge:
The patient was discharged in stable condition with instructions on wound care and symptom management.

Follow-Up Instructions:
The patient was advised to contact his primary care physician for any concerns or questions. He was to schedule a follow-up appointment with the surgeon within four weeks post-discharge to monitor the surgical site and assess any further symptoms.

N/A

1. Patient is a 23-year-old male with biliary cirrhosis presenting with abdominal pain and jaundice.
2. Laboratory findings showed elevated bilirubin, AST, ALT, coproporphyrin in stool, and uroporphyrin in urine.
3. Abdominal CT demonstrated hepatosplenomegaly with collateral vessels.
4. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy revealed esophageal varices.
5. Blood tests confirmed high levels of liver enzymes and bilirubin.
6. Post-liver transplant procedure led to severe sensory and motor polyneuropathy.
7. Post-operative complications included worsening liver function and fever.
8. Patient died on post-operative day 104 despite initial improvement.
records.source_note:
HOSPITAL COURSE SUMMARY:

Admission: A 23-year-old male with a history of biliary cirrhosis and recent episodic abdominal pain was admitted to the hospital with abdominal pain and jaundice.

Diagnostic Tests: During the workup, abdominal CT revealed hepatosplenomegaly with collateral vessels and esophagogastroduodenoscopy revealed esophageal varices. The patient's blood tests also revealed high levels of bilirubin, aspartate aminotransferase, and alanine aminotransferase. He also had elevated levels of coproporphyrin in the stool and uroporphyrin in the urine.

Procedure: Due to acute liver failure and intra-abdominal bleeding causing hypovolemic shock, the patient was listed for an emergency liver transplant. The procedure was successful, but the patient developed post-operative complications, including severe sensory and motor polyneuropathy. The patient's post-LT liver function tests initially improved, but worsened again, and were accompanied by fever about 1 month later. Despite our best efforts to improve his condition, including the administration of antibiotics, he developed multi-organ failure and expired on post-operative day 104.

Summary: The patient was admitted with abdominal pain and jaundice due to previous biliary cirrhosis. The patient underwent a successful liver transplant but developed severe sensory and motor polyneuropathy in the post-operative period. Despite our best efforts to improve his condition, including the administration of antibiotics, the patient developed multi-organ failure and expired on post-operative day 104.

Discharge Summary

Patient Name: Anonymous

Medical Record Number: [REDACTED]

Admission Date: [REDACTED]         Discharge Date: [REDACTED]

Admitting Diagnosis: None

Discharge Diagnosis: Subdural empyema with organized chronic subdural hematoma

Brief Summary of Hospital Course:

A 72-year-old man with well-controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus and implantable cardioverter-defibrillator implantation for Brugada syndrome was admitted to the hospital with fever and subsequent seizure in the left upper extremity. CT scans revealed asymptomatic chronic subdural hematoma, which remained unchanged over the past 2 years with conservative management. The patient was negative for human immunodeficiency virus and was not immunocompromised or had not been given immunosuppressive drugs.

The patient underwent a craniotomy under general anesthesia. After the dural incision on the subdural mass, a thickened, hardened, and yellowish outer membrane of the hematoma capsule was observed. When the outer membrane was incised, pus was collected. The inferior component of the subdural hematoma consisted of an organized hematoma. The inner membrane of the capsule strongly adhered to the underlying cerebral cortex. The organized hematoma and hematoma capsule were not removed to prevent injury to the cortex and spread the infection into the extracapsular subdural space. The definitive diagnosis was intracranial subdural empyema with organized chronic subdural hematoma.

Histopathological analysis of the outer membrane of the hematoma capsule revealed fibrous hypertrophy and inflammatory changes. The pus and swab culture observation period was extended to 14 days, and no growth of H. cinaedi was observed. Drainage for 10 days and antibiotic intravenous infusion therapy for 4 weeks resulted in normal serum C-reactive protein (CRP) levels. The patient was discharged without neurological sequelae and continued to receive oral minocycline (200 mg every 12 hours), leading to complete resolution of the subdural empyema 6 months postsurgery.

The patient was instructed to follow up with his primary care physician for wound healing and to monitor his diabetes and Brugada syndrome. The patient was also advised to continue taking oral minocycline for the recommended duration.

Patient Name: N/A

Summary:

The patient was a 35-year-old male with a medical history of arterial hypertension, left total hip replacement for avascular necrosis, and chronic convulsive syndrome. He was admitted due to progressive memory impairment, left hemiparesis, and language disorder. A brain biopsy revealed necrotizing granulomatous vasculitis.

Autoimmune, infectious, and malignant diseases were ruled out, and treatment with cyclophosphamide and methylprednisolone was initiated. The patient returned to the hospital two years later with aggressive behavior, mutism, incontinence, and progressive neurological deterioration. A new brain MRI showed two frontoparietal and left cerebellar inflammatory lesions compatible with the progression of the vasculitis.

Despite treatment with methylprednisolone and rituximab, the patient's condition continued to deteriorate, and he unfortunately passed away.

In conclusion, the patient had a history of multiple medical conditions and presented with neurological symptoms. After a brain biopsy, he was diagnosed with necrotizing granulomatous vasculitis and received various treatments. However, despite medical intervention, the patient ultimately passed away.

7. She had normal PT and aPTT with elevated lactate.
8. Initial workup for sepsis and adrenal insufficiency was negative.
9. Influenza and COVID-19 tests were negative.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Medical Record Number: [REDACTED]
DOB: [REDACTED]
Gender: Female
Admission Date: [REDACTED]
Discharge Date: [REDACTED]
Admitting Diagnosis: Altered mental status, hypotension, and fever
Final Diagnosis: Immunotherapy-induced RTA

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 68-year-old female with a medical history of metastatic melanoma, hypertension, deep vein thrombosis, and pulmonary embolism with inferior vena cava filter placement, was admitted with altered mental status, hypotension, and fever. She had recently received her second dose of immunotherapy with ipilimumab+nivolumab.

Upon admission, the patient's vital signs were significant for blood pressure of 75/40 mm Hg, heart rate of 110 beats per minute, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 95% on room air, and temperature 98.4 F. Physical exam revealed altered mental status, moderate respiratory distress, and bilateral lower extremity edema. Initial blood work showed Hg 10.3 g/dL; WBC 13.9 K/mcL; Platelets 164 K/mcL; Na 133 mEq/L; K 3.1 mEq/L; Cl 110 mEq/L; HCO3−1 mEq/L; BUN of 23 mg/dL; Cr 3.2 mg/dL; Plasma Glucose 103 mg/dL; Total Protein 5.0 g/dL; Albumin 2.6 g/dL; AST 737 U/L; ALA 399 U/L; ALK 99 U/L; Total Bilirubin 0.6 mg/dL; Direct Bilirubin 0.4 mg/dL; Calcium 7.3 mg/dL; Magnesium1.5 mg/dL; Inorganic Phosphorus 2.5 mg/dL; Procalcitonin 59.11 ng/mL; Lactic Acid 1.7 mmol/L; PT 17.7 SEC/INR 1.46; aPTT 49.2 SEC; COVID-19 PCR negative; SARS-CoV-2-IgG negative; Influenza Type A negative; Influenza Type B negative; Venous blood gas: pH 7.24, pCO2 of 24 mmHg.

Throughout the hospital course, the patient was managed for sepsis with multiorgan failure in the setting of a new RTA. Differential diagnoses included sepsis, adrenal insufficiency, antimicrobial toxicity, and immunotherapy adverse effects. The patient was initiated on a course of antibiotics and stress dose hydrocortisone with appropriate fluid resuscitation. Infectious workup, including computed tomography abdominal and pelvis w/o contrast, urine culture, blood cultures, chest x-ray, and transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE), was unremarkable.

On tapering the stress dose hydrocortisone, the patient developed transient hypotension, fever, and transaminitis episodes, thought to be related to immunotherapy. The patient was started on prednisone and transitioned to sodium bicarbonate tablets. Repeat blood work revealed an appropriate response with downtrending liver enzymes and increased serum sodium bicarbonate.

The patient was followed up with nephrology and oncology as an outpatient. She completed a prednisone taper over four weeks and denied symptoms at the follow-up encounter.

Discharge Medications:
-Sodium bicarbonate tablets

Follow-up:
The patient will follow up with nephrology and oncology as an outpatient.

1. The patient is a 39-year-old male presenting with low back pain and chest pain.
2. He developed enlarging soft masses in the plantar side of his right hallux.
3. Laboratory findings included normal calcium, low phosphorus, elevated alkaline phosphatase, and high FGF23 levels.
4. Imaging confirmed tumors in the right hallux responsible for FGF23 overproduction.
5. Systemic venous sampling verified elevated FGF23 levels in major veins.
6. Surgical resection of the tumors led to a significant reduction in FGF23 levels.
7. Phosphorus levels normalized after surgery.
8. Pain improved gradually and fully resolved by discharge.
9. Follow-up appointments are recommended.
records.source_note:
Hospital Course:
The patient was a 39-year-old male who presented with low back pain without any identified cause, as well as chest pain, right hip pain, and bilateral foot pain. One year later, he developed enlarging soft masses in the plantar side of his right hallux. The patient had no family history of metabolic bone diseases. Upon initial lab testing, the patient had normal calcium levels, but low phosphorus levels and elevated alkaline phosphatase levels. Further testing revealed a significantly elevated level of FGF23, indicating the possibility of TIO.

After additional testing, the diagnosis of TIO was confirmed, with the tumors in the right hallux expected to be responsible for overproduction of FGF23. A systemic venous sampling was conducted to measure the FGF23 in the patient's right common iliac vein and right external iliac vein, which confirmed the diagnosis. The tumors of the flexor tendon were resected, along with a tumor found in the first distal phalanx. Histological examination of the tumors showed oval-shaped mesenchymal cells densely packed in a fibrous background. Mitotic activity and necrosis were absent.

Post-surgery, the patient's serum FGF23 levels dramatically decreased from 215 pg/mL to 47 pg/mL, with phosphorus levels returning to normal. The patient's pain gradually improved over the course of two months and had fully resolved upon discharge.

Discharge Summary:
The patient was a 39-year-old male who presented with low back pain and developed enlarging soft masses in the plantar side of his right hallux. Diagnosis of TIO was confirmed with elevated levels of FGF23 and tumors seen on imaging. Resection of tumors resulted in a significant decrease in the patient's FGF23 levels and resolution of pain. Follow-up appointments are recommended.

Discharge Summary:

Admission Date: 09/30/2006
Discharge Date: 10/04/2006
Length of Stay: 4 days

Patient: 24-year-old woman

Admission Diagnosis: Myalgia, leukocytosis, neutrophilia, and monocytosis

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted to investigate an attack of muscle pains with associated myalgia, leukocytosis, neutrophilia, and monocytosis. She had a temperature of 38°C and elevated levels of C-reactive protein, ESR, and creatine kinase. Upon examination, she had marked tenderness of forearm, thighs, and calf muscles, and there were no significant findings otherwise. Blood tests showed an elevated CK, leukocytosis with neutrophilia and monocytosis, and a blood film showed occasional atypical mononuclear cells with some rouleaux. Her mid-stream urine showed a high white cell count, epithelial cells, and lactobacillus at >100 × 106/litre.

During her hospital course, the patient underwent a biopsy of the right tibialis anterior muscle that showed marked interstitial inflammation mainly by CD4 lymphocyte in association with occasional fiber necrosis, consistent with multifocal myonecrosis.

She was discharged in stable condition on 10/04/2006 with a follow-up appointment with her primary physician, and further investigations ongoing.

Discharge Instructions:

- Continue taking prescribed medications.
- Maintain a healthy and balanced diet.
- Follow up with primary physician as advised.
- Take rest as needed.
- Report any worsening symptoms to primary physician.
